Early Development of Communities A variety of economic, social, technological, and political preconditions are required before large numbers of people can live permanently in the same location. The first requirement is for a stable and abundant supply of food. Once humans mastered basic farming methods using early stone implements, they could develop more permanent residences. Once these methods were refined and produced a surplus of food, these residents could begin to trade with other populations for other goods. The existence of a surplus of food also provided the opportunity for involvement in other non food producing activities. For example, early communities began to diversify and further develop opportunities for specialization and trade. Early towns were ruled by a combination of military and religious leaders. These authoritarian leaders were successful at building irrigation systems, temples, palaces, and monuments and at designing systems that yielded agricultural surpluses that supported trade and the amassing of wealth by a few. Lewis Mumford, a renowned urban studies expert, wrote that t he first cities were the centers and the ceremonial complexes of very hierarchical societies. They housed the social elite, the granaries, the temples and the palaces; as well as enslaved masses of humans . Few early cities have left a more enduring historical legacy than ancient Athens. Athens was unique because its political system was based on municipal autonomy and democracy. Democracy comes from the Greek demos, meaning people, and kratos or power. Democracy is about power or the rule of the people the structure and process of governance depends on decisions that the people take. Polis, the Greek word for city, is part of the words metropolis and politics. The city was the fundamental level of politics and government in ancient Greece. The Athenians believed in an active, participatory form of democracy now referred to as sortition (Meslin, 2019, 304). In modern terms, we would say that ancient Athens was governed by direct democracy. They established a system whereby a small group of citizens governed themselves and the city. Each year a group of citizens were randomly using a machine called a kleroterion, a strange machine carved out of solid rock and full of hundreds of small slots, each filled with a small token bearing someone's name. White and black balls fell randomly through a pipe and dictated which tokens were chosen (Meslin, 2019, 304). If your token was chosen, you were a member of the council or leadership body similar to the cabinet in our parliamentary system (although it is important to note that these citizens were randomly selected and not elected like MPs who form our cabinet). These council members were entitled to speak, debate, and vote in the city s highest law-making body, the Assembly. This random selection of citizens to govern the city didn t last and in the end Athens had a military ruler like the other Greek cities. Nonetheless, its legacy has been powerful. First, Athens showed that large cities could be directly governed by their own citizens. Second, Athens had an important impact on thinking about land use and design. Many cities followed the example of Athens and built prominent public squares, usually part of their city hall buildings, as a gathering or meeting place for citizens. Finally, Athens serves as an example that even cities that claim to be practicing democracy may be systematically denying groups of residents access, influence, and participation in the political system. Athens gave the right to participate in the Assembly to a small group of men excluding women, people born outside Athens, and slaves living and working in Athens. It distinguished between citizens and non- citizens a challenge that we continue to face today in trying to describe the people who live in municipalities. Early Colonial Communities The English and French developed commercial and trading centres, military bases, and governance administrative centres to support their colonies. These early towns, often predated the formation of rural communities. Maurice Careless , a Canadian historian, argued that urban places have always played important leadership roles in directing the flow of population, economic activity, and culture in Canada. Canada s first centres had their systems of government determined by the French and English powers. In New France, the colony was ruled by a governor and council that was appointed by France. These representatives made sure that local residents paid their taxes, put in their compulsory days of service to build roads and other infrastructure, and complied with other rules related to trade. The British also had a centralized colonial administration structure, which was run by governors and councils appointed by Britain. The governors appointed local magistrates with responsibility for developing and enforcing local laws, and for taxing residents for the provision of local services. These magistrates were appointed for life and were accountable to the governors and not to the local citizens in the community. Canada s First Charter City Saint John, New Brunswick reached a population of more than 14,000 people in the 1780s . The need for local services and authority led the residents to petition the governor to incorporate Saint John. In 1785, nearly 50 years before any other town in British North America, Saint John was given a royal charter to become a charter city. Saint John is the oldest incorporated city in Canada and one of a handful of cities established by royal charter. Other charter cities include Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver, and Lloydminster, which is between Alberta and Saskatchewan. This first effort at incorporation was important because it defined municipal boundaries and it gave the municipality powers to tax residents and borrow funds. It created an elected council, comprised of a mayor and councillors, to make laws on behalf of the municipality and defined the right to vote for adult males who owned property valued above a minimum value. Pressures for Change There was growing pressure to get rid of the magistrate system from residents and landowners who resented paying taxes and having no say in the management and delivery of services. The British resisted, influenced to a large degree by their experience with the American Revolution they didn t want local governments to be a forum for local political mobilization. The American Revolution resulted in a large exodus of United Empire Loyalists from the United States to British North America. Over time, pressures for change in how the settlements were governed mounted from this and other new settlers from Europe. Between 1812 and 1850, Canada received over 800,000 immigrants, escaping the famines in Ireland and the impacts of the Industrial Revolution in Britain . These migrants put significant pressure on the towns and on the ability of the governor and magistrate system to continue to provide essential services. Services like roads, water supply, and law and order were strained. An outbreak of cholera in 1834 resulted in large numbers of deaths Montreal lost nearly 15 and Quebec City lost 10 of its population to cholera (Rutty and Sullivan, 2010, viii). As cholera spread, local boards of health were appointed and funded to manage the disease... colonies, streets and alleys were cleaned of filth and rubbish, pools of stagnant water were emptied and blocked drains were cleared, especially in areas were poor immigrants lived in crowded, filthy conditions. (Rutty and Sullivan, 2010, viii) Residents were increasingly unhappy with how they were being governed and rebellions in 1837 convinced the British that a new system was needed and they introduced incorporated municipalities in the 1830s and 1840s to upgrade local services and restore stability. The Foundation The Baldwin Act, 1 After the rebellions in Upper and Lower Canada, Britain asked Lord Durham to make recommendations on the future of government in the provinces. His 1839 report recommended the formation of a system of municipal or local self-government and the unification of Upper and Lower Canada. Lord Sydenham, who replaced Durham in 1840 as Governor-General, agreed with the recommendations to establish a system of local government. Both leaders were ignored the Act of Union in 1840 did not provide for the establishment of local authorities. In 1841, Sydenham convinced the newly unified province to allow elected district councils some delegated authority for administration and services like roads, taxes, education, justice, and welfare through the District Councils Act, but oversight and control rested with the representatives of the colonial powers. In 1849 the Municipal Corporations Act, or Baldwin Act (named after Robert Baldwin, its principal architect), was passed. Before the act, municipalities had to petition the colonial representatives for additional powers, responsibilities, and institutions and wait for approval through a specific statute. The passage of the Baldwin Act in Ontario had a significant influence on the development of local government to the present. While the focus was on making the colonies more efficient and effective, it was nonetheless the first piece of legislation to create a system of municipal government over an entire province. The Baldwin Act: authorized the creation of municipal corporations to manage local government; created a two-tier system of county government; created local councils as the municipal governing body (members of council were to be selected on the basis of election by eligible voters); stated that municipal councils should receive delegated authority from the provincial legislature and be subject to its control; recognized that urban and rural governments were separate with different powers among cities, smaller settlements, and rural townships; restricted local right to vote to property owners reinforcing the orientation of municipal provision of services to property and control by the elite; authorized municipalities to collect property taxes as their chief source of revenue; and involved increasing municipal responsibilities in relation to servicing and or regulating property. The Baldwin Act was the first legislation in the English-speaking world to consolidate in a single document a comprehensive legal framework for all forms of general-purpose local government, both urban and rural (Taylor, 2019, 49). In 1867, the British North America Act created the new country of Canada and established two levels of government in Canada that we have today the federal and provincial territorial. As discussed in Module 1, the BNA gave authority to provinces over local government. Following confederation, provinces began to define the types of municipal government structures such as townships, counties, districts, etc. and local residents could ask their province to incorporate their community into villages, towns, and cities based on the population in the community. It is interesting to note that if the British had acted on Durham s and Sydenham s recommendations to establish local government and include it as a form of government in the Act of Union, the BNA Act would likely have described three levels of Canadian government, not two. Unlimited Growth and Early Reform Efforts The period from the 1890s to about 1914 was a time of industrialization and rapid population growth in Canada. Again, the growth created pressure for changes to the system of local government. From 1901 to 1914, Canada led the Western world in rate of population growth. Between the census years 1901 and 1911, the population grew from 5.3 million to 7.2 million an increase of 34 in ten years. Most of the increase came from immigrants, many of whom settled in western Canada. Winnipeg, Calgary, and Edmonton grew significantly during this period, although other cities received large increases as well. City services and resources were strained. There were housing shortages, unsanitary conditions, unsafe drinking water that led to the spread of communicable diseases like typhoid, flu, and tuberculosis. As well, more residents met the property qualification required for voter eligibility and the balance of power began to shift from the elite and most affluent property owners. Three sets of early reforms were pursued in response to these growth-related urban problems: city beautiful, city healthy, and city efficient. City beautiful reforms engaged architects, engineers, and others who worked to create places of civic pride, including public squares, public buildings, and monuments. Healthy city reforms focused on public health such as sewers, fresh water, and housing standards. City efficiency reforms were strongly influenced by businesses with an emphasis on efficiency and professionalism. John Ross Robertson, a wealthy and influential newspaper publisher, commented that municipal government is a question of business not politics (Tindal and Tindal, 1995, 58). Reforms were also made to the structure, policies, and principles of local government. In some instances, responsibilities were transferred to other local decision-making bodies, known as special purpose bodies , to reduce the scope and responsibility of local government and the opportunity for political corruption. Officials were appointed to manage the range of special purpose bodies, including police commissions, hydro commissions, boards of health, and boards of education. These reforms served to strengthen the bureaucracy or staff side of the local government by establishing a type of city manager position to run the business of city hall and to introduce a merit principle into the hiring of public employees. Towns, which had been previously divided into wards with local councillors, were challenged to move to at-large elections or a town-wide elected board of control. Elected representatives, or councillors, were to be hands-off ; their power and influence was reduced. The emphasis on business was evident in policy-making and towns actively competed for business, jobs, and a strong tax base. Post WWII Suburbanization The period after World War II was a time of further municipal restructuring. Again, rapid population growth from immigration and the post-war baby boom put pressure on municipalities in and around urban areas of Canada. The population growth brought distinct changes to the pattern of development and put pressure on rural areas near cities. Supported by increasing car ownership, the construction of major highways such as the 401 in 1959, and a general sense of economic prosperity, development moved to areas farther and farther from the central city into suburbs. Suburban development has arguably been the single most powerful influence shaping Canadian society in the second half of the twentieth century. It has certainly been the single most important influence in shaping our cities . Rapid suburbanization created a number of challenges for local governments across Canada. Suburbs, developing in rural areas on the the outskirts of urban centres, were not equipped to provide the range of infrastructure and services required by this new population, nor did they have the property tax base to support such service and infrastructure expenditures. On the other hand, there were fears that business would avoid the suburban community if it didn t improve its infrastructure and services, adding to its financial challenges. Often the suburbs were not well connected to the city, and roads and transit lines had to pass through a number of municipalities to reach the city, which created new coordination and jurisdictional problems. Suburbanization changed the core city as well. The city of Toronto s population declined between 1945 and 1953 while suburbs on the borders of Toronto increased by about 200,000 people (City of Toronto, 2006). This type of loss and growth was mirrored in other large cities. the tax base of the cities because as businesses and residents moved to neighbouring suburbs with lower property tax, there were calls for lower tax rates within the cities. The movement of the middle class to the suburbs began the process of geographic polarization based on income and opportunity that we see reflected within our cities today. There was also pressure on the planning, funding, and delivery of services, in particular those which crossed boundaries, such as transportation, or those like road systems that had a spillover benefit. Urban municipalities became interested in expanding and there were pressures to annex suburban municipalities into the urban areas to help increase their tax base and support the needed large-scale infrastructure projects. When annexations took place, there was often a shift in the power balance in the municipality as the urban core was outvoted by the suburban representatives on council. Reform and New Structures These pressures led to a second wave of municipal reforms. By the early 1950s, the City of Toronto had burst its relatively compact boundaries (City of Toronto, 2006) and petitioned the province to amalgamate the 12 outlying municipalities into one city with a single mayor and municipal council. Not surprisingly, the 12 suburbs argued against this proposal (Levine, 2014, 204). The province agreed that change was needed but took a different path than that requested by the city; in 1953, the province established the first two-tier metropolitan government. Other provinces followed Ontario s example and in 1970, Quebec established the Montreal Urban Community as a two-tier federation of the City of Montreal and its 29 neighbouring municipalities. Similar systems were set up for Quebec City and Hull. In 1965, British Columbia established regional districts as their two-tier framework for local government. In British Columbia, it was up to the municipalities in a district to decide what powers to transfer to the upper-tier region, resulting in a two-tier system where the local governments were the strongest. The Greater Vancouver Regional District included 20 municipalities in the Vancouver area. Key Point A two-tier municipal structure includes local, lower-tier municipalities and some form of regional or upper-tier municipality. Local municipalities have responsibility for local services, such as local parks, local streets, and libraries, while the upper level oversees regional services like water, regional roads, planning, and infrastructure. All local municipal council members and mayors are directly elected and some regional councillors are directly elected as well. In this case, the municipal ballot provides the opportunity for voters to elect local representatives as well as regional representatives. In other municipalities, regional representatives are indirectly elected in this case, the local council may appoint one or more local councillors to also sit on the regional council. Often, the regional councillor, whether appointed or directly elected, is a member of both the local (lower-tier) and Two-tier municipal structures contrast with one-tier structures. Tindal . describe two types of one tier structures lower-tier only (found in Prince Edward Island) or upper-tier only (for example, Ottawa or Toronto) (2017, 114 115). We don't generally refer to Toronto or Ottawa as upper-tier - instead we call them single or one tier municipalities that have sole responsibility for their assigned functions in their geographic area. Some provinces rejected the two-tier model. Winnipeg became a two-tier regional government system in 1960, but the city and nine municipalities were amalgamated into a single-tier municipality in 1972 to address city-suburb conflicts and disputes. The new Winnipeg unicity combined the city and the suburbs in one municipal council of 50 members. Resident advisory groups were established to provide citizen input into local decision-making, although these were later abolished, and the council size was reduced. Calgary and Edmonton followed the unicity approach and annexed suburbs to their city. New Brunswick provided another alternative. That province chose to assume some traditional responsibilities of local government in education, public health, and welfare rather than address issues related to the structure of local government. As you will learn a bit later in the module, this was part of a disentanglement initiative and is an example of uploading. The 1960s were a time of optimism, rebellion, and protest about inequality, rights, as well as development. Local municipalities felt the impact of the protests against large-scale development of city areas, like the proposed Spadina Expressway in Toronto, and other urban infrastructure developments. Citizens expressed their desire to be part of local decision-making beyond the ballot box at election time. Reform and Annexations As growth continued, many municipalities were bursting at the seams. Provinces continued to consider amalgamation of municipalities as a response to pressures of growth. Municipalities often dealt with growth-related pressures by annexing land from neighbouring municipalities to the urban area. In Ontario, the Ontario Municipal Board heard over 400 applications for annexation in the 1950s and 1960s (Meligrana, 2000, 8). City of London The City of London, Ontario, experienced a 7 increase in population between 1951 and 1956. Neighbouring townships increased between 45 and 66 over that period, and by 1956, they were home to about a quarter of the population of the county. The City of London was home to about half the population. (Meligrana, 2000, 8) London provided water infrastructure to the surrounding townships and argued that it needed additional developable land to help pay for new infrastructure. It was competing with other cities for economic growth and needed additional land to support growth and development. Over the years, various annexation proposals were brought forward . In 1953, the City of London s request to annex land from neighbouring townships received a positive decision from the Ontario Municipal Board . The next step was for the Ontario government to pass legislation to approve extending the city of London s municipal boundaries. Political maneuvering from a Member of Provincial Parliament, representing one of the townships affected by the decision, resulted in a much reduced annexation motion, and the annexation was put on hold by the province. (Meligrana, 2000, 12) Pressure continued to mount on London s municipal infrastructure and finances, and population growth and development continued in nearby municipalities. London engaged consultants to study the matter and again applied to the OMB for an additional 60,000 acres of land (Meligrana, 2000, 13). Again, the OMB supported the annexation, but sided with the townships in their request for a board of control four members who would be elected at large by all voters in the new municipality of London to ensure that the new township residents would have influence and voice in the new municipality. The annexation took place in 1961 and the city of London became home to about three-quarters of the county s population (Meligrana, 2000, 8). However, the newly annexed townships had significant populations and power and replaced the mayor with a township candidate in the first election after annexation. Some inter-municipal regional structures were introduced at the same time. A planning board was established in 1962 to advise on developments in the Central Middlesex area, including London and neighbouring townships. The London Suburban Roads Commission was established with a responsibility to oversee the planning and maintenance of county roads (Meligrana, 2000, 17). Reform and Disentanglement The challenge of servicing urban growth continued to exert pressure on the structure and boundaries of municipalities. Rural to urban migration, immigration, and general population growth as well as efforts to attract business and economic development and compete globally required new infrastructure and additional services and programs. All had to be supported from a limited property tax base. Canada experienced a recession in the early 1980s and again in the early 1990s, which put further pressure on municipal finances to support services and programs. The federal, provincial, and territorial governments experienced similar financial pressures and undertook reviews of their role and scope in an effort to reduce spending. Over time, many services became entangled among different levels of government, with each playing a role in service delivery and often sharing in the cost of providing these services. This led to some duplication of effort, inefficiency, and often resulted in conflict among the levels. Disentanglement was a process by which the levels of government reviewed their roles and responsibilities and determined who should have responsibility for the program. Many provinces, particularly in Ontario and Nova Scotia, undertook who does what? exercises to review and negotiate disentanglement with municipalities. Disentanglement is based on the principle of subsidiarity or assigning authority for services to the level of government most appropriate for providing that service. For example, subsidiarity would mean that responsibility for a national service like defence would be best held at the national level, while maintaining a neighbourhood playground and park would be a municipal responsibility. Disentanglement took three forms: Uploading when the responsibility for a service or program was assumed by the upper level of government Downloading when responsibility was given (or downloaded) to the municipality with the resources to provide the service or program Offloading when responsibilities are given to municipalities without any or even sufficient resources or funding Disentanglement was complicated by finances. In Ontario, the who does what exercise was described as zero-sum meaning that the realigned responsibilities would not result in additional costs or benefits to either the province or the municipality. Of course, this was hard to do and necessitated modelling, forecasting, and negotiation about the value and anticipated cost of service responsibilities to ensure that there were no gains or losses. While there were significant disentanglement efforts in some provinces in the 1990s, there continued to be calls for reviews of municipal responsibilities related to the delivery of provincial programs. These calls stemmed from downloads that were implemented without sufficient funding and which became a Recently, some have called for reviews in light of the financial implications of COVID-19 on municipalities, arguing that this is a time for a systematic review of the role, authority, and financial capacity of municipalities. The Millennium and Continued Reform Looking back on the discussion so far, we can see a consistent rationale used to justify the various reform initiatives across the country. They include: Efficiency and costs to save money by improving efficiency, achieving greater economies of scale, and reducing duplication Political ideology to reduce bureaucracy, reduce government, and reduce red tape Service delivery to realign the municipality to better reflect the current form and size of the urban area and to provide for coordinated service delivery Control sprawl to control sprawl by expanding the boundaries and planning jurisdiction for the area Improve competitiveness to compete globally by reducing internal competition and coordinating infrastructure and services needed by businesses and investors Reduce inter-municipal conflict to eliminate conflict between municipalities Enhance equity to address equity issues in the property tax system and among suburban and core communities through a larger and more stable tax base These continue to influence initiatives to reform the structure and function of local government in Canada. And there are some additional reasons. The turn of the millennium period constitutes another important modernization initiative designed to help municipal governments, and to some extent their respective provincial and territorial governments, deal with challenges posed not only by demographic, economic, and social factors in the domestic and international environments, but also their own past policy decisions and those of other governments within the Canadian and international political systems. (Garcia and LeSage, 2005, 8) Garcia and LeSage argue that the pursuit of recent municipal reform is an effort to improve governance. They note that municipal calls for greater autonomy from the province and or constitutional recognition, as well as the need for improved relationships between municipalities and provinces, have influenced recent initiatives. Municipalities are limited in their ability to grow, compete, and provide good quality of life for community members due to constraints on their authority and capacity. Past downloading and disentanglement have resulted in less than positive relationships with the provinces. At the same time, questions are raised about connections with local communities and residents, and about engagement, access and responsiveness, and accountability. Calls for municipal reform are also influenced by an increasing interest in democracy and representation at the local level (Stoney, 2006, 108) and in the desire for an improved relationship with communities and community members (Garcia and LeSage, 2005, 15). The millennial reforms have included a similar range of elements as earlier reforms : Structural reform amalgamations, deamalgamations, the creation of one- or two-tiered structures, the establishment of inter-municipal coordinating bodies, annexations Functional reform realigning who does what and disentangling Financial reform through disentanglement initiatives, expanding municipal revenue sources, changes to property tax systems Many have also included an additional element: Jurisdictional reform reviewing the scope of municipal power and authority. Many provinces introduced new municipal acts, giving municipalities natural person powers. Some established charters or unique legislation, such as the City of Toronto Act or the Halifax Charter. We can see some evidence of these reforms in most provinces, although they pursued different reform paths and the level of reform varied from tinkering to significant. Few of the reforms were as extensive as recommended in the original reform reports. Amalgamation and New Structures No discussion on the history and development of municipal government in Canada would be complete without a discussion of the amalgamations that occurred in the late 1990s and early 2000s. These reforms could be a module themselves, and this section provides a very high level overview of select large municipalities. The textbook discusses the changes in more detail. Metropolitan Toronto, with a metropolitan or regional level and six area or local municipalities (Toronto, Etobicoke, East York, York, North York, and Scarborough), was created in the late 1950s but was dissolved in the late 1990s. Ignoring widespread protest and criticism, the Ontario government announced that the two-tier municipal government structure (known as metro government) would be replaced by a consolidated one-level city the new city of Toronto, or the mega-city, as it was known. While the change happened as of January 1, 1998, the process of amalgamation and harmonization took many years. Like previous amalgamation efforts, the changes were undertaken to reduce costs, improve governance, reduce the size of local government, and improve efficiency and accountability. Montreal also had a two-tier structure of local government in the late 1990s. The Montreal Urban Community was the regional level and 28 local municipalities (including the city of Montreal) formed the local or lower level. In 2002, these municipalities were amalgamated into a new city of Montreal. The new city included 27 new boroughs for local matters and was part of the Montreal Metropolitan Community , which included 82 municipalities in the Montreal area. Like the Toronto amalgamation, the goals included efficiency, consistency of services, improved clarity of governance, and better accountability. Some suggest that there were political motives related to reducing Anglophone municipalities (Trent as referenced in Harris, 2013). As well, the amalgamation was designed to better respond to globalization forces by centralizing decision-making and sharing costs more equitably across the region. Similar to Toronto s amalgamation, Montreal s was very unpopular. The 2 Quebec election included a promise by the elected Charest government to allow municipalities to hold a referendum whether to de-merge. Twenty-two referenda were held in 2004 in municipalities now part of Montreal; 15 voted in favour of de-merging. In 2006, further changes were made to the structure of local government in Montreal. In a nutshell, the City of Montreal continues to have authority over the remaining 19 boroughs, which continue to have their own local councils. In addition, there are 15 reconstituted municipalities that are again separate from the city, although they have fewer powers than they did originally. An agglomeration council, including the City of Montreal and the 15 municipalities, was established to coordinate key services like police, water, and transit. While it is a coordinating body, rather than a formal level of local government, it is not without criticism. The de- merged municipalities complain that they are getting a raw deal and that they pay significant amounts of their property tax revenue to the agglomeration council for regional services; they have asked for voting weight on the council. In 1996, the province of Nova Scotia amalgamated the cities of Halifax and Dartmouth, the town of Bedford, and the Halifax County municipality a collection of urban, suburban, and rural communities. Again, there was significant opposition to the amalgamation. There remains considerable mixed opinion on the various amalgamations and whether they have been successful or not. Some of this opinion is influenced by the strong resistance to the amalgamations to a one-tier city. Montreal , Toronto , and Halifax amalgamations all included sizable populations that represented a large proportion of the total population of their province. Analyses have not provided evidence of cost savings or efficiencies after these amalgamations. In fact, most studies suggest an increase in wage salary costs, which are a significant portion of the municipal budget. It often takes years to harmonize policies, systems, structures, and human resources in the newly amalgamated cities. There is still competition among municipalities Toronto area municipalities still compete with one another for business and economic development. In addition, there is still resentment, conflict, and frustration between and among municipalities and communities affected by restructuring Montreal provides a good example of the ongoing discussion about power and finances. A 2018 survey in the Halifax Regional Municipality reported that 48 of residents overall (54 in urban areas) want the regional municipality separated into urban and rural municipalities . Charter City Status and New Powers The earlier section of this module talked about charter cities, established by the Queen to provide early forms of governance in the colonies. Charter cities are being proposed once again as a way to address the challenges of limited power granted to cities under current provincial legislation. A charter city designation moves a city municipality out of the Municipal Act and establishes special provincial legislation unique to that municipality, allowing more flexibility and typically giving broader powers authority. Charter city legislation generally includes a clause that recognizes the city as an order of government and commits to intergovernmental consultation with the municipality. Vancouver was an early charter city, with legislation passed in 1953. Since that time, the old Municipal Act was replaced by a new Municipal Act and a Community Charter , both of which contain updates like natural person powers and spheres of jurisdiction that apply to other municipalities but not to Vancouver. Originally, the City of Winnipeg had additional revenue powers, but they were given to all municipalities in a 1997 update to the Municipal Act. Winnipeg has responsibility for policing, and its capital borrowing is reviewed once a year by the Department of Finance, whereas other municipalities have to get approval from the Manitoba Municipal Board. The City of Toronto Act was passed in 2007, the same year that the province also approved changes to the Municipal Act. Toronto has additional revenue taxation powers, has debt financing tools, and is required to have an auditor general and ombudsperson. The mayor has some additional powers. In 2008, provincial legislation in Nova Scotia established the Halifax Charter. It makes sense for Halifax, as the province s largest city, its economic engine, and its capital, to have its own charter legislation as stated by the provincial minister responsible for municipal affairs (Nova Scotia, 2008). The legislation gives Halifax additional general powers, increases the requirement for ministerial approval of long-term borrowing from 100,000 to 500,000, allows the municipality to form district councils, and imposes a requirement that the province consult the city prior to making any amendments to the charter (Nova Scotia, 2008). Edmonton and Calgary negotiated charter city status with Alberta in 2018. Their agreement included a fiscal framework, policy tools that provide increased flexibility and authority, and agreement regarding participation in charter collaboration tables with the province . Cape Breton Regional Municipality is interested in charter city status. Reporter David Jala, from the Chronicle Herald interviewed Mayor Cecil Clarke in January 2020: David Jala: As mayor you have favoured the establishment of a charter specific to the Cape Breton Regional Municipality. What is the status of the proposed charter? Mayor Clarke: My initial intent with the charter was to give us the legislative tools, to give us Crown authority, to make some decisions that would impact us locally without it applying to Halifax has a charter and thus has the ability to be flexible and get things done because they can change some of the structural elements in it. It may end up that the charter is the best route, but for the past several years the province has been a review of the Municipal Government Act and at this point there are no wholesale changes. An update of the Act may give us what the charter could achieve, but a challenge that we face as a regional municipality is that we are not structured like a town or a county and we have a different reality as we are comprised of eight former municipal units and that s where having a charter could help us respond better to some of the challenges we face. Some argue that granting charter city status gives municipalities much needed power and authority, however, it can also be argued that it doesn t make much difference because the additional powers and authorities are limited, and experience has shown that even when cities have additional revenue tools they don t use them consistently. Harry Kitchen argues that charter city status has largely been a myth when it comes to cities accessing and implementing new taxes . Provinces are reluctant to give charter cities additional powers and when cities get them (i.e. Toronto) they are reluctant to use them. Moreover, the example of Vancouver shows that charter city legislation that is out of date compared to other municipal legislation can be limiting for the charter city. Continuing Change The discussion of the growth and structure of local government in Canada is complicated by economics, public opinion, finances, and politics; therefore, it is important to recognize that it is not static it is an evolving work in progress. Boundary changes may continue in the city of Ottawa based on scenarios associated with their Ottawa 2 Growth Plan . The scenarios developed by City of Ottawa planners contrast intensification with the need for annexation of some neighbouring land in order to accommodate the anticipated growth under the scenarios. Saskatchewan had 283 municipal annexations between 2001 and 2016, British Columbia had 212, and Alberta had 210 . Between 2006 and 2010, nearly a quarter of municipalities in Alberta were involved in municipal annexations it will be interesting to see if this changes in the future . Residents of Toronto were surprised by the mid-2018 election decision by the Ontario government to reduce the size of city council from 47 to 25 members, especially as the city spent nearly two years considering the size of council (given the growing city) and necessary ward boundary adjustments based on development and population growth. This provincial change was undertaken for greater efficiency in decision-making and to save money on Toronto governance Toronto council was described by the Premier as bloated and inefficient . Toronto has challenged the decision in the court system and the outcome is pending. Ontario also announced plans to review regional, two-tier government in January 2019. Two advisors were appointed to make recommendations to the Minister of Municipal Affairs on eight regional municipalities that include 74 lower-tier municipalities in an effort to improve local accessibility, efficiency, and effectiveness that respects taxpayers money ; reduce red tape and duplication; save costs; and create an openness for business . Later in 2019, the Ontario government advised that it would not be requiring changes to the regional, two-tier government structure in Ontario. Instead, it announced a fund to allow municipalities to find better, more efficient ways to deliver their services, including structural and boundary changes and a requirement that regional municipalities review the size of their council. Some municipalities, like Muskoka Region, recognize the fund as a prod to consider future change and municipal-led amalgamations may be anticipated in the future. A similar path has been followed in Nova Scotia. The Minister of Municipal Affairs is encouraging municipalities to consider governance and structural changes to maximize resources for municipal services. Municipalities are amalgamating the Region of Windsor and West Hants was established in April 1, 2020, because of a merger between the two neighbouring municipalities. The mayor of the Town of Shelbourne, which is part of other discussions about possible amalgamation, commented that if the talks fail to materialize and produce a merger the town would be forced to apply for dissolution . Village Resists: The Forced Municipal Mergers of Quebec is an interesting documentary on the forced mergers and subsequent de-amalgamations in Quebec. You are encouraged to watch it if you want to learn more about the local politics behind the complex amalgamation processes in that province. Right Size? Fundamental to the discussion of municipal reform is the question of the right size. Most of the reforms were based on research and analysis into the right size for municipal functions, services, and programs. Many also considered parallel goals of representation, engagement, and healthy local democracy. The tension between efficiency and representation is a theme in these questions. The amalgamation of Toronto was supposed to result in more efficient services across the city; the establishment of local community councils was designed to bring local decision-making closer to community members to counterbalance the size of the new city (which is larger than a number of provinces). Is There a Right Size? Some argue that bigger municipalities encompassing the full geographic community are better. They can be more efficient and take advantage of economies of scale. There is less spillover other municipalities or residents of neighbouring municipalities benefit from services without paying taxes and contributing to the cost of the service in the host municipality. Larger municipalities support an expanded and more professional public service that has the capacity to do research on policy options and use evidence to inform decisions. Nevertheless, advocates for smaller municipalities argue that this structure provides for a greater connection and engagement with local community members. There is understanding of the local issues, residents can contribute their experience and local knowledge, and there are more opportunities for an active civil society engaged in local democracy. Of course, neither small nor large municipalities are perfect. Small municipalities can be insular and limiting and protect those with power and privilege. Larger municipalities can be anonymous, providing little connection to communities and people. Questions about the right size have been asked for hundreds of years. People were asking, even in the 1830s and 1840s, what geographic areas would be best suited for the emergent functions of local government? (Magnusson, 2015, 9). They have influenced discussions about municipal boundaries and annexation, amalgamations, disentanglement, as well as municipal financing. Subsidiarity, the principle of lowest level possible, is informed by an understanding of the right or best size for service delivery. Unorganized Territories Before we conclude this discussion, it is important to remember that our experience of municipalities is not shared by everyone. While there are 444 municipalities in Ontario, about 82 of the province and 33,000 people are not part of a municipality . They live on unorganized land called Some of these are territories belonging to First Nations or First Nation reserves, but others are lands that are not part of an incorporated municipality. Services are delivered to non First Nation unorganized areas through regional service boards. For example, the District Social Services Administration Board delivers social services and emergency services and other regional services. Residents who live in unorganized areas pay a land tax to the province that is lower than property taxes paid by residents living within municipalities, reflecting the lower level of services in those unorganized areas. TWOMOs may border existing municipalities. Like the earlier discussion of residents moving to suburbs to benefit from lower property taxes, residents of municipalities may choose to move outside their municipality to a TWOMO for the same reason. They may also resist annexation efforts by municipalities that may want their boundaries to reflect the actual community and built area. Pause and Reflect At the beginning of the module you were asked to look at the history of your local municipality and how it has changed since it was first established. How many of the reforms described in this module had an influence on your municipality? Reflect on why the change happened when it did, and why it took the particular form that it did. Where do you see it heading in the future? Are there possible changes on the horizon? For example, how will technology continue to shape our definition of community and the structures and shape of local government? Key Takeaways There are some important takeaways from the discussion of the history, development, and reform of municipalities and local government. Senior and more powerful levels of government have always set the basic rules for local government. Canadian municipalities have never been able to determine their own roles, powers, and government structures. We will learn later in the course that this pattern continues. in Plain View: Local Agencies, Boards, and Commissions in Canada Jack Lucas Department of Political Science, University of Toronto IMFG perspectives 2 About IMFG The Institute on Municipal Finance and Governance is an academic research hub and non-partisan think tank based in the Munk School of Global Affairs at the University of Toronto. IMFG focuses on the fiscal health and governance challenges facing large cities and city-regions. Its objective is to spark and inform public debate, and to engage the academic and policy communities around important issues of municipal finance and governance. The Institute conducts original research on issues facing cities in Canada and around the world; promotes high-level discussion among Canada s government, academic, corporate and community leaders through conferences and roundtables; and supports graduate and post-graduate students to build Canada s cadre of municipal finance and governance experts. It is the only institute in Canada that focuses solely on municipal finance issues in large cities and city-regions. IMFG is funded by the Province of Ontario, the City of Toronto, Avana Capital, and TD Bank Group. Author and Acknowledgements Jack Lucas is a PhD candidate in the Department of Political Science at the University of Toronto and a 2012-2 Graduate Fellow at the Institute for Municipal Finance and Governance. In his doctoral research, Jack is exploring the history of local special purpose bodies in Canada with a focus on processes of institutional change. The views expressed in this paper are those of the author and not IMFG or its funders. Munk School of Global Affairs, University of Toronto 1 Devonshire Place Toronto, Ontario, Canada M5S 3K7 Copyright held by author, 2013 0-7727-0918-1 Executive Summary Many of the most explosive local controversies today spending scandals, service disruptions, political disputes share one thing: they involve local agencies, boards, and commissions (or ABCs). In Toronto, controversies about waterfront redevelopment, libraries, public housing, and transit planning have been complicated even caused by the ABCs in these fields. The same is true in many other Canadian cities. This should not come as a surprise. Everywhere we turn in municipal politics, from transit to housing, conservation to libraries, education to policing, we encounter ABCs: local or regional public agencies, with a single or limited set of functions, that receive their revenue partly or wholly from municipal governments, provincial governments, user charges, or some combination of these. These ABCs (or special-purpose bodies ) provide hugely important services, spend large sums of money, and raise serious questions about democratic accountability. Yet we spend little time thinking about how they are governed. Supporters of local ABCs argue that some services should be kept at arm s length from municipal politics and that ABCs allow certain operations to be governed by those with an interest or expertise in the field, rather than by municipal politicians. Those who oppose ABCs argue that they keep local councils from coherent budgeting, priority-setting, and policymaking and that ABCs are nearly invisible to the public, making important decisions without sufficient local oversight and accountability. This paper poses three practical and important questions. The first concerns existence: do we need to have ABCs at all? The second is about scale: what is the appropriate geographic boundary (local, regional, provincial, etc.) for a particular policy task? The third is about personnel: who should sit on the board of the ABC and should they be appointed or elected? We consider each of these questions in light of experiences with local ABCs in Canada and abroad. IMFG Perspectives 1 Hidden in Plain View: Local Agencies, Boards, and Commissions in Canada Introduction At the bottom of Cherry Street, on an ordinary summer morning, the city of Toronto seems a world away. Early risers walk dogs through the cool lakefront air. Gravel trucks rumble past. Tourists loiter at the water s edge, their cameras pointed at the skyline across the harbour. Standing in the sand at Cherry Beach, looking across at the morning roar of the city s downtown expressway, visitors could be forgiven for thinking that they had stumbled into a completely forgotten world. In August of 2011, however, this small corner of the city was anything but forgotten. That month, local media reported that members of the city s executive committee had plans to transform the city s waterfront redevelopment program. Naturally, the headlines focused on the striking new suggestions for the waterfront: a monorail link to the downtown, a massive shopping mall and waterfront hotel, and the world s largest Ferris wheel. But the real debate that summer and the question that Toronto s council was required in September 2011 to answer was whether responsibility for redevelopment in the Port Lands should be transferred from Waterfront Toronto, a tri-level redevelopment body, to Toronto Port Lands Co., a city agency. Waterfront Toronto, with four appointees each from the federal, provincial, and municipal governments, was criticized by some as being too distant from the city and too cautious for speedy action. A reorganized Port Lands Co., on the other hand, would have two municipal councillors on its board, along with two municipal bureaucrats and five council appointees, and would therefore be linked much more directly to Toronto s city council. For all the talk of shopping malls and Ferris wheels, the waterfront debate in summer 2011 was really a debate about special-purpose governance.1 Hidden in Plain View: Local Agencies, Boards, and Commissions in Canada 2 When we refer to local ABCs, then, we are speaking about public agencies of limited purposes, operating locally or regionally, that are more or less formally separated from the ordinary council-committee structure. The best-known special-purpose bodies have been around for decades, even centuries: school boards, library boards, transit commissions, and boards of health. In many municipalities, however, special-purpose bodies have proliferated. In Toronto, for example, they range from the massive Police Services Board to much smaller operations like the William H. Bolton Arena Board of Management. The fiscal arrangements for local special-purpose bodies also vary widely. In councils have the final authority to approve the budgets of special- purpose bodies. But this authority is a matter of degree. In some cases, such as libraries, council can review and adjust the board s submitted budget.5 In other cases, like policing, council can approve or reject a budget, but it cannot specify particular items that the board should increase or decrease.6 And in the peculiar case of school boards in Ontario, council is required by law to levy taxes on behalf of the board, but has no control over the board s budget.7 In many cases, local boards also receive funding from the province, and particular tasks and services are often mandated and funded, wholly or in part, by the province. Whatever the fiscal arrangements, however, the money involved is no small matter: in many Canadian cities, more than a third of the city s operating budget is handed over to special-purpose bodies every year.8 Consider Vancouver. In 2012, of the city s 1.1-billion operating budget, 243 million more than a fifth of the budget was devoted to policing; a further 103 million was budgeted for parks and 42 million for libraries. These three policy areas are administered by special-purpose bodies and, in the case of parks, by a separately elected Park Board. The three ABCs alone represent more than a third of Vancouver s operating budget, not to mention thousands of its employees.9 Moreover, a full account of local spending by ABCs in Vancouver would include regional bodies such as Vancouver Coastal Health (health care) and TransLink (public transit). How ever we do the calculations, in other words, we find enormous public funds under the control of Vancouver s local and regional ABCs. The same is true in many other Canadian cities. ABCs provide very important services, spend large sums of money, and raise serious questions about democratic accountability. This was not unusual. Everywhere we turn in municipal politics, from waterfront redevelopment to libraries, transit to housing, education to policing, we encounter a peculiar administrative animal: the special-purpose body. These ABCs of local government agencies, boards, and commissions are more than mere administrative quirks, confined to a few forgotten corners of the local landscape.2 They provide hugely important services, spend large sums of money, and raise serious questions about democratic accountability. But what are they? How do they operate? And why might we defend or deplore them? In this paper, we will provide a toolkit for thinking about local ABCs for anyone who wants to understand the strengths, weaknesses, and purposes of local special-purpose bodies in Canada. If our goal is to understand and improve Canada, we cannot afford to ignore these local special-purpose bodies. What are local special-purpose bodies? The first challenge in any discussion of local special- purpose bodies is that the enormous range and variety of ABCs, each with its own peculiar history, makes them difficult to summarize. When a group of Canada s leading experts on local ABCs met some years ago to write a book on the subject, they found that the task of defining the special- purpose body was more difficult than they had expected.3 Still, it is useful to have some definition of the ABC in mind. In my view, the best definition can be found in a decades-old report by Susan Dolbey of the Government of Ontario, who defined local special-purpose bodies as follows: (1) They are public bodies in that they are either elected by local voters or appointed by council(s), the provincial government, or other special- purpose bodies (2) They operate at the local or regional level, but outside the normal council structure (3) They have a single function or a limited range of functions (4) They receive at least part of their revenue from and or user charges.4 IMFG Perspectives 3 Thinking about Local ABCs: Three Key Questions Across Canada, thousands of local ABCs are performing important tasks in dozens of widely varying policy fields. Are they improving local governance, or worsening it? If we decide to create or reform local ABCs, where should we begin? To clarify our thinking on these issues, there are three general questions that we need to ask about special-purpose bodies. They concern existence, scale, and personnel. 1. Should the ABC exist? The first question is the simplest: should the ABC exist? While advocates and critics of special-purpose government have made many arguments for and against local ABCs through the decades, there are a few arguments to which those on both sides of the debate have returned again and again.1 Those who advocate local ABCs often claim that a particular service, such as policing, should be insulated from local politics, either because the service is too important or complex, or because it would create conflicts of interest or patronage if councillors were allowed to control the service directly. In some cases, this is cast as an argument for efficiency: by separating particular services from councillors who might impede or micromanage them, tasks like policing, utilities, or transit can be operated in a more efficient and businesslike manner.1 This argument emerged in Canada s urban reform era , but it is still alive and well today. Do not leave the future of our city to our city council, wrote Toronto columnist Royson James during the 2011 waterfront debate. Too many of the councillors too often don t know the details of an issue, fail to understand the core principles governing many policies and are like a political weather vane that spins in the direction of the prevailing political power source. 1 If we allow our politicians to get too involved, the argument goes, our policies will suffer from short-term, inefficient, and excessively political thinking.1 Better to entrust those areas to special-purpose ABCs. A second, related argument is that local ABCs provide an opportunity to recruit people into public service who might not otherwise be involved. There may be people with particular interests, acumen, or expertise who would not seek municipal office, but might be willing to sit on the board of a special-purpose body. Historically, this argument has been used to justify the recruitment of businesspeople for businesslike services (like utilities) and experts for scientific services (like planning). But it could as easily be used to justify the need for environmentalists on waterfront commissions, poverty activists on housing corporations, or What is central to the argument is the belief that some policy areas should be overseen by those with a special interest or expertise, rather than by uninterested or uninformed local politicians.1 Of course, many disagree with these arguments and not just the municipal politicians who are implicitly or explicitly besmirched by them. Those who oppose special-purpose bodies often begin with the problem of fragmentation. If we create local ABCs to administer particular tasks, they argue, no one body or agency will be able to make coherent decisions for the city as a whole. How, these critics ask, can a city like Toronto develop a coherent waterfront policy, when responsibility for the waterfront is divided among a conservation authority, a port authority, a tri-level waterfront commission, and three levels of government? The same criticism could be made of transit policy, urban homelessness, health care, and a range of other issues. For critics of local ABCs, it is better to empower a general-purpose government a municipal council, a regional government, or the province with enough authority to make policy decisions across a range of fields and to the basis of the needs of the community as a whole. A second common argument against ABCs concerns accountability. When a policy is the responsibility of council, the lines of praise and blame are usually clear. But the same cannot be said of local ABCs. If a conservation authority makes an unpopular decision, who should be held responsible? If local residents object to the sums being spent on policing, or transit, or housing, to whom should they complain? Recent research on the Toronto waterfront has suggested that special- purpose bodies can sometimes be so distant from ordinary lines of accountability that they virtually constitute a separate, unelected level of government.1 Even in less extreme cases, the lines of responsibility and accountability can be perplexing for careful observers and altogether bewildering for the general public. The result, according to critics, is a system of local policymaking that would score low on any reasonable evaluation of democratic accountability. In addition to these common arguments for and against local ABCs, there are many others, pertaining to particular services, in particular places, at particular times. Speaking generally, however, local ABCs are often supported by those If we allow our politicians to get too in- volved, the argument goes, our policies will suffer from short-term, inefficient, and excessively political thinking. Hidden in Plain View: Local Agencies, Boards, and Commissions in Canada 4 who are focused on a single local service, such as hydro, planning, or conservation, who hope that a local ABC will protect and insulate the policymaking process in their favoured domain. Those who care passionately about public libraries, say, but have little interest in municipal government in general, may defend the existence of their local library board. Those who are more concerned about the operation of local government in general, on the other hand, tend to be more skeptical.1 Advocates of localism, who believe that local communities should be empowered with more autonomy, tend to be critical of specialized ABCs. Ultimately, then, our answer to the first question about existence depends on our reaction to these broader arguments for and against local ABCs. But we must remember that there is nothing natural about the arrangement of local special- purpose bodies in Canada today. Some policy tasks that were once thought to require special-purpose administration, such as water distribution and urban planning, have been safely under the control of municipal councils for decades. In many jurisdictions, tasks like policing, education, and watershed management are carried out by general-purpose municipal, regional, and provincial or state governments rather than ABCs. When we compare ourselves to other jurisdictions, in other words, we quickly realize that our way is not the only way: we might choose to create ABCs similar to those being used effectively in other jurisdictions, or we may realize that certain ABCs can safely be eliminated. Like most organizations, public and private, special- purpose bodies are easier to create than to eliminate. When the legislation to permit library boards was first passed, for example, it provoked almost no debate or discussion. But legislation to abolish library boards would surely provoke a passionate reaction. Once they are created, special-purpose bodies quickly gain important resources that help them survive over time: local clients who become accustomed to interacting with an ABC rather than with council; inter- municipal and inter-provincial organizations in which members of local ABCs meet to discuss and coordinate their policies; provincial departments whose officials prefer to work directly with specialized local agencies; and, of course, politicians of every stripe who cry local autonomy! whenever reforms are proposed. When we are considering a new special-purpose body, therefore, we should ask ourselves if we want the new special-purpose body to persist for ten, twenty, even fifty years into the future. 2. What s the right scale? Suppose we decide that an ABC does deserve to exist. Our next question might concern scale: what is the best geographic boundary for the ABC? In theory, the possible answers are limitless, but in practice, the choice is restricted to three options. First, a special-purpose body might be located at the municipal scale, sharing a border with a single municipality. Many well-known ABCs, such as library boards and planning commissions, are organized at the municipal scale. If the local scale is too restrictive, we might consider the regional scale, larger than a single municipality but smaller than the province as a whole. In some cases, such as policing and education, a regional ABC might share a border with an upper-tier municipality like a county or a regional government. In other cases, like conservation or public health, the boundaries of the regional ABC might be drawn exclusively for the purposes of a particular policy task. The range of possibilities at the regional level are nearly limitless, from smaller ABCs that incorporate just two or three municipalities, like a small utilities commission, to huge ABCs, like Conservation Authorities, whose geographic territory sometimes includes dozens of Among the policy fields in which regional ABCs are employed, one recent area of innovation has been in public transit: in the past two decades, several of Canada s largest cities including Vancouver, Toronto, and Montreal have created regional public transit agencies.1 The third scale is provincial. Many hundreds of ABCs operate at the provincial scale, performing a wide range of tasks, and we can occasionally find calls for a particular local service to be relocated to the provincial level. During recent debates on hydro distribution in Ontario, for example, some argued that the province should create a single distribution Like most organizations, public and private, special-purpose bodies are easier to create than to eliminate. IMFG Perspectives 5 utility to cover the entire province.1 Others have made similar arguments, with varying success, in the areas of public health, water treatment, and education. When it comes to scale, the story of the past century in many policy fields, such as education, public health, and policing, has been one of consolidation. In an attempt to capture economies of scale, to simplify the administrative system, and to build agencies with the capacity to carry out highly specialized modern services, local ABCs once bounded by a single municipality have been consolidated into much larger boards at the county, regional, or mega-regional level. In many cases, consolidation began as a voluntary local option, stimulated by funding incentives from the provinces. Provincial governments have often found it easier to introduce and defend a voluntary approach, rather than face the charges of centralization that inevitably accompany mandatory changes to entrenched local institutions.1 We must remember, however, that voluntary consolidation is rarely a panacea for policy problems, and the result is almost always a system that is more complicated than the one it replaced. No matter how attractive the incentive, some municipalities will choose not to consolidate, leaving some parts of the province under the old form of administration and others under the newer consolidated structures. In Ontario, for example, voluntary consolidation programs in education and public health resulted in adoption rates of roughly 50 percent that is, half of the province s local governments decided not to adopt the new structures which made governance, accountability, and funding all the more complicated. More recently, a voluntary consolidation program in hydro has resulted in a handful of very large utilities, a number of mid-sized utilities, and a few extremely small distributors. The current hydro system in Ontario is arguably as difficult to coordinate as the system it replaced. Consolidation is rarely painless. There is no easy path to regional ABCs, and if the process is to be completed, compulsory legislation will probably be necessary. If the goal in a consolidation process is to simplify the administrative landscape, only compulsory consolidation, with all of its political risks and challenges, is likely to make such simplification a reality. 3. Should ABC boards be elected or appointed? Finally, we must also ask: who should govern the ABC? Who should sit on its board? How and by whom should senior staff be appointed? Answering these questions requires that we decide, first of all, whether members should be elected or appointed. These days, with just a few exceptions such as school board trustees or the Vancouver Park Board most ABCs are governed by appointed board members. If we decide that an ABC should be elected, however, there will be further decisions to make. Will the board members be elected in wards, or at large? How many will be elected? For how many years will they serve? These questions could be answered in a thousand ways, but those who have supported elected ABCs throughout Canadian history have typically advocated at-large systems with relatively lengthy terms of office in an attempt to insulate the ABC from parochial and short-term thinking. If we decide that an ABC should be appointed, we also face a host of questions. First, we will need to decide who gets to make the appointments. In many cases, board members are appointed by municipal councils, but some appointments are also made by provincial governments (e.g., some boards of health), by outside associations (e.g., local heritage boards), and even by other ABCs (e.g., some library boards). A second councillors to serve on the board. Some local ABCs are composed entirely of making them very similar to committees of council; in others, one or two councillors are selected along with a handful of non- politicians; and sometimes, councillors are forbidden from These eligibility rules often appear poorly thought- out at one point, Ontario had two sets of provisions for creating local park boards, one requiring local councillors, and the other forbidding them and it is useful to think very carefully about the nature of the people who sit on the board. In general, provincial statutes have grown more flexible on this issue over time, giving local councils more freedom to decide whom to appoint to their local special-purpose bodies. The most obvious consideration to keep in mind when thinking about personnel is insulation: how closely should the ABC be linked to the municipal council? As we have seen, a common argument for local special-purpose bodies is that they insulate sensitive tasks from the local political sphere. In many cases, this claim is accurate: mayors and councillors often pay little attention to the day-to-day decisions of their conservation authorities, library boards, or transit commissions. When those bodies make more far-reaching or controversial decisions, however, the insulation provided by the ABC structure often proves to be very drafty indeed. And they raise ongoing questions about accountability and efficiency, flexibility and independence, fragmentation and oversight. Local ABCs have been with us, in Canada, for more than a century. For an early negative statement in the Canadian case, see Harry Kitchen, Some Orga- nizational Implications of Providing an Urban Service: The Case of Water, Canadian Public Administration, , : 297 308; for a more positive view, see Mark Sproule-Jones, The Recent events in Toronto provide examples of this problem. On the one hand, local politicians rarely hesitate to get involved in a policy issue, even when the issue has been entrusted to an agency, board, or commission. From policing to transit to housing, local councillors feel free to make criticisms and suggestions, even when they are not directly involved with the relevant ABC. On the other hand, when controversies do arise within special-purpose bodies controversies from which local politicians might prefer to be insulated it is rare that they avoid blame. Controversies in Toronto about social housing, for example, have spilled over into council debates, despite the insulation that is supposedly provided by the Toronto Community Housing Corporation. The insulation provided by local ABCs often seems to break down precisely at the moments of heightened controversy for which it was created. If the goal is to insulate a policy arena from local politics, other options such as a transfer of responsibility to a regional or provincial government might do the job in a more lasting and effective way. A Final Observation At the end of September 2011, the waterfront controversy that had been boiling in the city of Toronto was back to a simmer. Despite their strenuous efforts, those who had advocated for the proposed changes failed to secure enough support to transfer responsibility for the Port Lands from Waterfront Toronto to the Toronto Port Lands Co. In the end, council voted only to speed up the redevelopment process along the waterfront. Although Waterfront Toronto survived, the debate in summer 2011 illustrated the accountability and governance challenges that are ever present in the relationship between municipal governments and ABCs. The story of Toronto s 2011 waterfront debate illustrates a final, very simple observation about local ABCs in Canada: each of them has its own story. The more that we investigate the history and organization of local ABCs, the more we realize that we are dealing with an extraordinary variety of very different species. Special-purpose bodies can be local or regional, elected or appointed, fiscally independent or dependent, publicly prominent or largely invisible. They can be large or small, permanent or temporary, prestigious or pilloried. While all of them might be accurately defined as special-purpose bodies, there is as much that differentiates these agencies, boards, and commissions as unites them. The role of special-purpose bodies in local governance is significant and under-appreciated in Canada. Email: Funding information Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada, Grant Award Number: 890 2018 0 Abstract While past research suggests that informal processes of dialogue play an important role in municipal inter- governmental relations in Canada, we currently know very little about their character and frequency. Who do local elected officials communicate with, and through which channels? And which municipal voices carry the most weight in these conversations? This article answers these questions from the perspective of elected politicians themselves, using a pan Canadian survey of municipal, provincial, and federal elected representatives. Our find- ings confirm that municipal intergovernmental relations depend heavily on informal institutions and personal relationships and highlight the key role of municipal mayors as spokespersons and advocates for municipalities in Canadian federalism. Et quelles voix Par Nos r sultats INTRODUCTION Canadian political leaders routinely acknowledge that municipalities deserve a seat at the table when federal and provincial governments meet to discuss issues relevant to cities and local communities. But Canada's federal institutions do not include any formal mechanisms for intergovernmental collaboration or shared decision making with municipal governments . processes and personal relationships between municipal mayors and councillors and their parliamentary counterparts . We currently know very little about these informal mechanisms of elite intergovernmental communication and advocacy. How often do mayors and councillors actually interact with provincial and federal officials? Who do they communicate with most frequently? Which municipal voices carry the most weight in these conversations? In this article, we aim to answer these questions using a new survey of municipal, provincial, and federal elected representatives across Canada. We use the survey data to describe municipal provincial and municipal federal relationships from the perspective of municipal mayors and councillors themselves, while also comparing municipal representatives' perceptions to those of their provincial and federal counterparts. We begin by reviewing the academic literature on Canada's federal institutions, both formal and informal, then explore the historical and present role of municipalities and municipal elected representatives within these institutions. Next, we present survey results that help illuminate the mechanics and defining features of multilevel governance in Canada. Our findings demonstrate the importance of informal processes of intergovernmental communica- tion and advocacy in the Canadian municipal sector, and highlight the especially important role of mayors as spokespersons and advocates for their municipalities. We show that provincial and federal politicians generally share municipal representatives' perceptions of these relationships, further cementing the importance of informal relationships in municipal intergovernmental interaction. Throughout our analysis, we also find that municipal population size is strongly associated with municipal representatives' perceptions of both the quality and the character of intergovernmental interaction in Canada.
