Please do not redistribute CHAPTER Future Prospects for Municipal Governments T he future for local governments in Canada will be more activist. Frances Frisken once noted that Canadian municipalities often used the lack of jurisdictional authority as an excuse for inaction. 1 The past decade has suggested a significant attitudinal change in such local governmental thinking. Examples, large and small, abound-from the commitment to \"fair trade\" in Wolfville, Nova Scotia, to the establishment of North America's first official supervised injection site in Vancouver, British Columbia. Leading up to the 2015 federal election, Canada's municipalities stepped forward offering to take and help settle Syrian (and related) refugees- though municipal fiscal reality meant that many local governments acknowledged that their offers were partly contingent on federal immi- grant settlement aid. On environmental matters, many municipalities have signed on to Kyoto targets on emissions, not waiting for senior governments to lead with their own action. Municipalities, such as Burnaby, BC, have indicated they will take whatever local action they can-including civil disobedience-to stop the development of Kinder Morgan's Trans Mountain Pipeline and oil sands bitumen shipping in their communities. Apart from the designation as Canada's \"best run municipality,\" Burnaby Mayor Derek Corrigan and his fellow Burnaby Citizens' Association councillors stand out as dedicated, committed, local representatives and as electoral examples with a history of democratic success through this local engagement. 1 Frances Frisken, ed., The Changing Canadian Metropolis: A Public Policy Perspective, Introduction, Berkeley, CA: Institute of Governmental Studies Press, University of California, 1994. 3 In 2014-2018, British Columbia became the last Canadian province to institute four-year terms of office; given the senior trend of fixed- usually four-year-terms provincially and federally, this longer local governmental planning horizon may push the political professionalism of councillors and councils from a more part-time orientation. While sometimes adding recruitment challenges for smaller municipalities, the shift to longer council terms also raises questions about ensuring accountability, a feature largely answered with the development of local political parties. While for most Canadian local governments, this latter development remains uncertain, there is no doubt that local governments in Canada will be more engaged. How well municipalities fare in the 21st century will depend, as always, on how successfully they maintain a balance between their two primary roles: representative political and administrative service delivery (see Box 12.1). The tension between these two roles is reflected in two contrasting images of municipal government-as a democratic institution that responds to community concerns, and as but one of many players in a competitive marketplace in which individual interests prevail. This book began with fanciful suggestions about the 21st century belonging to Canada's municipalities. What have we learned in the more than 400 intervening pages that support or detract from this optimistic outlook? NEl Chapter 1 Future Prospects for Municipal Governments 3 What needs to happen if this new century is to bring greater municipal significance? Taking a New Look The best way to start, especially for those in municipal government, is to turn upside down the usual way of looking at municipalities, a perspec- tive that has them on the bottom of several levels of higher jurisdiction, as in Figure 12.1. According to this traditional view, municipalities are subordinate and subservient creatures of the provinces to which they owe their existence. They are also dependent on the federal (and provincial) levels for financial assistance that-in practice-is limited and elusive, and they are significantly affected by senior federal government actions (and inaction). They are also increasingly constrained by international agreements and organizations and by global competitive pressures and a prevailing neoliberal ideological paradigm. There is, however, an alternative way of looking at municipalities and their place in the world, unaccustomed as we are to considering it. What if we invert the traditional hierarchical view, as in Figure 12.2? What if we see local governments as the first order of government? Let us con- sider the significance of such a reversal. Globalization and the accompanying free trade regime are certainly forces to be reckoned with, but we shouldn't overstate their impor- tance for day-to-day municipal operations. Not all firms are completely mobile, and most would think long and hard before pulling up stakes and setting up shop in another country where culture, language, and other barriers may present quite a challenge. Since the terrorist attacks Figure 12.1 The Traditional Hierarchy International Agreements and Organizations I I I Federal Provincial Government Goverment I Municipal Government Figure 12.2 The Inverted Hierarchy Local Citizens I I Provincial Government I Federal Government I International Agreements and Organizations of September 11, 2001, many actions have been rationalized or justified \"because of 9 11\" or \"ISIS\" and its equivalents-no matter how tenuous the link. The attacks have become an all too convenient cover or excuse for actions (especially adversely affecting individual rights and free- doms-as in Canada's C-5 Anti-Terrorism Act of 2015) that would not otherwise be tolerated. In much the same way, globalization is constantly invoked as the reason why something must be done or cannot be done. Without in any way denying its importance, we should not allow it to become an excuse for municipal actions or inaction. There is still consid- erable scope for municipal initiative within a global world. It is instructive to examine Martin Horak's analysis of the background to Toronto's New Deal campaign that ultimately led to the new City of Toronto Act of June 2006. 2 At first blush, one might interpret this devel- opment as the inevitable response of a global city seeking out additional powers to strengthen its competitive position. But Horak found that the forces of global economic competition were not the key factors driving 2 Martin Horak, Governance Reform from Below: Multilevel Politics and the \"New Deal\" Campaign in Toronto, Global Dialogue Series, , Nairobi, ON-Habitat, 2008, accessed October 30, 2011 and July 3, 2015, at aspx?publicationiD 2494. A similar dynamic might occur among Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, Premier Kathleen Wynne, and Mayor John Tory for Toronto. Future Prospects for Municipal Governments 3 Toronto's New Deal campaign. Instead, he identified a number of devel- opments that came together to create the impetus and opportunity for change: The provincially imposed amalgamation that created the City ofT oronto; Provincial downloading of social programs that burdened the new municipality with substantial costs; and Elections at all three levels of government that resulted in leaders (Prime Minister Martin, Premier McGuinty, and Mayor Miller) predisposed to working together. The size of the amalgamated municipality gave it increased clout, and the disparities in downloaded cost burdens between the new City of Toronto and the suburban municipalities in the surrounding Greater Toronto Area provided further stimulus for those seeking greater powers for Toronto. The arrival of the \"three Ms\" as heads of the three levels of government provided the other major factor favourable to a New Deal for Toronto. Horak's research into the Toronto case demonstrates that even in cities that are highly integrated into the global economy, the exigencies of global competition are not the only or necessarily even the primary influence. He concludes, \"both the size of the new City and the sense of fiscal crisis that accompanied its birth were critical to the emergence of the New Deal campaign, in that they enabled and encour- aged the new City to move beyond the passive intergovernmental stance that Canadian municipalities have typically assumed given their weak standing in the constitutional order.\" 3 Once again, we have a welcome example of what \"eager beavers\" can accomplish. Though Meaghan Joy and Ronald Vogel offer caution in overinterpretation of the Toronto advantage. 4 Because the constraints imposed by globalization apply more to federal and provincial governments, it can even be argued that the net result is to liberate rather than to restrict municipalities. National borders are more porous and the nation state is challenged by international trade rules and agencies and scaled back by neoliberal preachings about the inherent superiority of private-sector operations. These global and ideological pressures affect the local level as well, but municipalities also have an opportunity to move into the vacuum created at the centre by the reduced role of the federal and provincial levels. In fact, the municipal capacity to capitalize on this opportunity has been strengthened, unwittingly, by the actions taken by the federal and provincial levels in response to global- ization and neoliberalism. JUNE 9, 2 BY ENID SLACK TOMAS HACHARD Saskatoon, Sask. Shutterstock.com Municipalities have played a central role in Canada s response to the COVID-19 pandemic. They have provided economic relief to residents and businesses, instituted public health measures, delivered vaccines and begun planning for a post-pandemic future. The increased cost of this work, combined with decreased revenues particularly from user fees such as transit fares have resulted in significant, unanticipated operating deficits. Large cities with transit systems have been especially hard hit. Because municipalities are required by law to pass balanced operating budgets every year, they have not been able to resort to more borrowing. Instead, federal and provincial governments have stepped in to help them cover the shortfalls. Alongside fiscal deficits, municipalities have also faced a governance deficit. While they have been on the front lines responding to the pandemic, they nevertheless have been excluded in many cases from key decisions made at the federal and provincial level. Instead, municipalities have relied on advocacy to get heard, although public health units have in some cases made use of their authority to enact certain restrictions. All of this points to an underlying reality about Canadian federalism. Despite the important role that cities play in the federation, local governments are equipped with limited sources of revenue largely property taxes, user fees, and transfers from the federal and provincial governments. They also do not have any real role or voice in Canada s federal structure and are generally not included in federal- provincial discussions or negotiations. Both of these problems need to be addressed. Municipalities should have access to the revenue necessary to fund the services they must provide. There should also be regular trilateral meetings among Ottawa, the provinces and senior municipal leaders to address issues of common concern, while recognizing the different needs of large and small municipalities. Municipalities have too often been the forgotten partners or little siblings of Canadian federalism. Recent research has highlighted the challenges Canadian municipalities face in this respect. Municipalities have a semblance of authority in several policy areas, but often little actual power to make changes unilaterally, partly because provinces have shown little interest in ceding control. They have inadequate revenue sources and insufficient fiscal flexibility to meet their responsibilities. There is often unclear and overlapping jurisdiction between municipalities, provinces and the federal government. Finally, much of Canada lacks appropriate regional governance structures to encourage inter-municipal co-operation. Coming out of the pandemic, there is an opportunity to put municipalities and Canada on firmer footing by addressing fiscal capacity and flexibility, embracing municipalities as partners and taking municipal differences into consideration. Address fiscal capacity and flexibility Provincial governments determine the revenue sources available to municipalities. They also hold municipalities to balanced budgets for operating purposes, and restrict how much they can borrow for capital expenditures. This high degree of provincial control ensures that municipalities maintain good fiscal health, but it can obfuscate real fiscal problems. Balanced budgets, for instance, can hide the fact that a municipality is unable to pay the cost of maintaining and building new infrastructure, including public transit and affordable housing, using revenue sources at their disposal. It will give you the opportunity to better understand your own municipality as well as understand how local government fits in to the bigger picture of governance in Canada. Key Point You have probably noticed that this introduction has used the terms local government and municipality. Local government is the lowest level of elected government in Canada. It is often used interchangeably with municipal government which is the type or form of local government. But local government can also include locally elected school boards as well as police boards and agencies, boards and commissions that have been established locally. Local government can be a confusing term referring to both the type of government (i.e., different from provincial or federal government) and the process of local decision-making, including all local boards and councils (Tindal , 2017, 2). Municipal government is clearer, referring to the elected municipal council and related corporation, although as we will learn later in the course, there are different forms and shapes of municipalities! It is also important to distinguish between government and governance. Government is the group of representatives elected to a defined, formal institution with authority to govern a community or area. Governance is a broader term that refers to the processes of governing and relationships between the formal institutions of government and civil society. Governance is about the interdependent relationships between and among different levels of government and other public, private, nonprofit, and community members that are involved in making and influencing how decisions are made. Civil society is another important term that refers to the sphere of social interaction between the economy and the state, composed of the family, voluntary associations, social movements and other forms of organization and communication among citizens. Civil society is created through the mobilization and actions of non-governmental actors but may be institutionalized by a variety of state and societal means (Graham, Phillips and Maslove, 1998, 286). Local government is one part of civil society and works with the others in a variety of ways, including the delivery of services, policy development, community development, and decision-making. This module will introduce local government what it is, why it is important, and why we need to study it. It will position local government in the governance structure in Canada and will distinguish roles and responsibilities of the different forms of government. Federalism and Governance in Canada Did You Know? Municipalities were created before many provinces were formally established and before Confederation. While the boundaries and structures have changed, local government as an order of government has been in existence a long time. Tindal, Tindal, Steward, and Smith trace the origins of local government back to 1647 in Quebec. For a period of about 27 years, locally elected syndics in Quebec City represented the concerns of the settlers to a colonial council that had been appointed by the king of France. The Municipal Corporations Act, 1849, or Baldwin Act, is generally recognized as the foundation of local government as we know it today. It allowed for the establishment of municipal corporations to raise funds through taxation, address local matters, and deliver local services. The other important foundation for local government is the British North America Act (now the Constitution Act, 1867), which established Canada and created a federation of two levels of government, national and provincial. : National National Federalism is understood to be a political system in which the powers of the state are formally divided between central and sub-national (or provincial) governments by a written constitution. These governments are linked in an interdependent political relationship. Canada recognizes the British Crown as the head of state. The role and powers of the national level of government are set out in Section 91 of the Constitution Act. The provincial or sub-national powers are defined in Sections 92 and 92A. It is important to note that in a federation, one level of government is not above the other each has a distinct set of powers and authorities, based on a division of responsibility for policy and program areas. Provincial Provincial You have probably noticed that local government is missing from the description of federalism that is because it is not recognized as a level of government in the Constitution Act, 1867. Key Point Section 92(8) of the Constitution Act assigns responsibility for municipal institutions to provincial and territorial governments provinces have the power to pass legislation that creates and establishes the structure of municipal government. This means that local governments are created by and subordinate to the provinces and are often referred to as creatures of the province. Most provinces have passed specific municipal legislation Ontario has the Municipal Act, S.O. 2001, which delegates power from the province to municipalities (formed by the province) in Ontario. Larger cities may have their own legislation for example, Vancouver has had a charter since the 1950s, Toronto is governed by the City of Toronto Act, S.O. 2006, and Alberta has approved charter city legislation for Edmonton and Calgary. While there is no one document that describes the relationship between the national and provincial territorial governments, many pieces of legislation define the relationship between provinces and their municipalities. The result is that there are many different systems, forms, and structures of the 3,500 municipalities across the country. The other important point is that municipalities are established as corporations this dates back to the Baldwin Act. Canada s national and provincial governments are part of a system of constitutional monarch where the head of state, Queen Elizabeth , has powers that are limited by the Constitution. Municipalities, in contrast, are corporations. Interestingly, as we will explore later in the module, they may not enjoy the power and authority of corporations; many municipalities have their powers and authorities defined and delegated by provincial governments. watching these videos. Pay particular attention to some similarities as well as some key differences between local governments in the two provinces as you listen to the discussion of the numbers and types of municipalities and their roles responsibilities, method of election (ward or at large), and structure of government (single-tier, two-tier, or regional districts). 1. The following table describes the responsibilities and authorities of each level of government. Municipalities have been included, even though they are institutions of the provinces territories but are not named in the Constitution, to show how the pieces fit together. Power to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of Canada except for subjects assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces. Limited to the powers explicitly given to them in the written Constitution. Established by provinces with a defined set of local responsibilities. The federal government can assume provincial responsibilities if it is for the general advantage of Canada, and they have scope to assume additional unassigned responsibilities. This potential to assume responsibility, if it is in the national interest, has been used by the federal government a number of times, including regarding atomic energy, the grain trade, and the 1940 constitutional amendment, which gave Parliament exclusive power over unemployment insurance . More recently, the federal government has assumed responsibility related to energy and climate policy. Although, the introduction of a federal cap and trade program has been challenged by three provinces in the courts with varying decisions on whether the federal government has the constitutional right to assume responsibility in this area. Provincial and territorial authority is more sharply defined and it is limited to the areas defined in the Constitution they cannot take over any federally designated areas of responsibility. However, the federal parliament can delegate the administration of a federal responsibility to the provinces and territories. Want to Know More? If you want to learn more, you are encouraged to watch Who Does What? , a light rap- based story of the division of responsibilities between the three levels of government. Municipal roles and jurisdiction are defined in provincial legislation, usually through a municipal act. Some provinces define specific responsibilities and authorities for local government in their provincial municipal acts, and if a municipality wants to get involved in an issue beyond their defined role and authority or in a new issue or program area that wasn t anticipated when the municipal act was written, they must ask for provincial permission. Other provinces include a general list of policy areas that aren t defined as provincial responsibilities or that municipalities aren t expressly prohibited from getting involved in. Natural person powers give permissive powers to municipalities to do things that ordinary persons can do. Halifax has been advocating for natural person powers for a number of years it is advocating to the province to amend its Charter to include these powers (for more information see the How Canadians Govern Themselves). Municipalities in various provinces including Ontario, New Brunswick, and British Columbia have natural person powers. Want to know more? Want to read more about the division of power and the different functions and responsibilities to the three levels of government? Here are two resources produced by The Library of Parliament: 1. How Canadians Govern Themselves 2. Our Country, Our Parliament Branches of Government Dyck describes government as the set of institutions that make and enforce collective, public decisions for a society. Political institutions provide the framework within which politics take place; these institutions structure the behaviour of the political actors, including voters, politicians, and bureaucrats. They provide a set of rules, roles, authority structures, symbols, and rituals. In Canada, these institutions are organized into three branches the legislature, executive, and judiciary. Did You Know? The executive branch, which includes the prime minister (or premier) and cabinet, has a wide range of powers, including setting the policy agenda for the government. In addition, the executive manages and controls where the government will spend money and oversees the bureaucracy, which advises on public policy, implements approved policies, and provides services as directed by the government. The legislature (or parliament) is made up of elected members who represent the people and play an important role in approving policy and passing laws. The judicial branch, or courts, increasingly interprets the laws (and approved policies) in the case of disputes between the state and interests. Local government is also different from federal, provincial, and territorial governments in terms of the structure of government and its institutions. Rather than having three separate branches, it combines both the executive and legislative roles, whereby the elected municipal council is responsible for developing and approving bylaws as well as overseeing the operations and administration of the municipality. Structure compares the parliamentary and municipal systems and explains why they are so different. Municipalities Municipalities vary considerably based on size, ranging from 100 residents to millions. They are called cities, towns, villages, regions, townships, districts, and counties. They vary significantly in their form and function from province to province and it is almost impossible to present a definitive picture or description of this level of government. Did You Know? The Resort Municipality of Whistler is a unique municipality that was established in British Columbia in 1975 with a focus on promoting, facilitating, and encouraging the development, maintenance and operation of a resort promotion area . The 2016 census reported that there were 5,162 municipalities in Canada (Statistics Canada, 2017, 1). Wikipedia reports 3,573, and a quick review of provincial and territorial websites listing the number of municipalities (as of February 2020) resulted in about 3,086. Confused? The number of municipalities may change depending on provincial restructuring initiatives and occasional requests from municipalities to amalgamate with other municipalities. In 2010, residents from the municipality of Canso in Nova Scotia voted to amalgamate with Guysborough County because of financial challenges related to a reduced tax base . Rocky Mountain House municipal council voted unanimously to pursue amalgamation talks with two neighbouring municipalities in late 2019 . Amalgamation is not always voluntary. Residents of Toronto, Ottawa, Windsor-Essex, Kawartha Lakes, Haldimand-Norfolk, and Hamilton were subject to amalgamations in the late 1990s and early 2000s despite their considerable opposition. Ontario announced plans to dissolve Peel Region - the Region will cease to exist in 2025. Brampton, Caledon, and Mississauga will be single tier cities. Prince Edward Island has been engaged in municipal restructuring a new municipality of West River was established from five existing municipalities, North Shore was established from an amalgamation of three municipalities, and Central Prince was established through an amalgamation of two municipalities (Prince Edward Island, 2018). Municipal Purpose As noted earlier, municipal purposes are defined in the provincial territorial municipal acts and generally include references to good government and accountability, the provision of services and facilities, as well as community safety and well-being. The Ontario Municipal Act defines municipal purposes as follows: Municipalities are created by the Province of Ontario to be responsible and accountable governments with respect to matters within their jurisdiction and each municipality is given powers and duties under this Act and many other Acts for the purpose of providing good government with respect to those matters. (Ontario, 2006, c. 32, Sched. A, s. 2) Manitoba defines municipal purposes as follows: The purposes of a municipality are a. to provide good government; b. to provide services, facilities or other things that, in the opinion of the council of the municipality, are necessary or desirable for all or a part of the municipality; and c. to develop and maintain safe and viable communities. (The Municipal Act. 1996. C.C.S.M. c. M225, clause 3) Local governments provide leadership in the community. They fund and provide services and are responsible for local economic development. They are institutions of local decision-making and provide a democratic base. They respond to the needs and the will of the people and they represent the community to other levels of government. Municipal Role Municipalities have two main roles service provision and political representation. The Provision of Services and Programs The service delivery role may involve delivering provincial services programs that have been set out in the Municipal Act or delegated or downloaded to municipalities by provinces or territories. The municipality may also decide to deliver services programs based on community need. Lightbody noted that local government is the one most directly relevant to a person s pursuit of a satisfactory life. From their early origins, municipalities have focused on service to property. The current definition of municipal responsibilities in Ontario includes the following: Protection services policing and firefighting Transportation services roads, expressways, and public transit Environmental services waste management and water supply Social and family services Ontario Works welfare assistance, childcare, and senior support Social housing Health services public health, education, and disease prevention Recreation and cultural services parks, community centres, libraries, the arts Planning and development regulating what can be built and where and promoting investment and business growth While municipalities may have formal responsibility for a function, they may not actually deliver the service. Many municipalities choose to establish a special-purpose body such as a transit commission, housing authority, or conservation authority to plan and deliver the service. Or they may fund others, through contract or purchase of service arrangement to provide the service on their behalf. In some municipalities, there are two levels or tiers of local government a regional and a local level. In these cases, responsibility for services with significant regional scope like policing, waste management, and social and public health services are assigned to the regional level, while more local services like recreation and libraries are assigned to the local level. A Political Role of Representation Local government provides a mechanism to identify and address collective goals and objectives within a municipality. This includes encouraging facilitating resident participation and engagement, advocacy related to municipal interests, and collaboration with other orders of government to meet municipal needs and interests. Local government is considered a model for citizen participation and engagement in democratic government. One of the most famous expressions of this view comes from the early 19th century and French political theorist Alexis de Tocqueville: Town meetings are to liberty what primary schools are to science; they bring it within people s reach, they teach people how to use it and how to enjoy it (de Tocqueville as quoted in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 2018). De Tocqueville was more impressed with the process of local government (how decisions were made) than with the outcomes (what decisions were made). He believed that direct democracy, where citizens make decisions in their own communities, was uniquely possible in the smaller scale municipal arena and that local governments were the best training schools for democracy. Local government is often described as open government. This means that municipal government is accessible to the public and that its actions are transparent. Municipal council and committee meetings are open to the public, residents have the right to make presentations to council and or its committees, there are requirements for public notice about meetings, there are conflict of interest policies, and there are procedural standards for the disposal of municipal properties. Most agree that local governments are uniquely suited to active participation by citizens. City hall is close to home, the mayor and councillors live and work in the community, and the issues often have a direct impact on the residents. However, as we will explore later in the course, others note that democratic local government is facing some challenges such as low voter turnout at municipal elections, underrepresentation of women and diverse candidates, and the excessive influence of certain groups on local decisions. Whose Interests Do Local Governments Serve? Whose interests do local governments serve? The quick and easy answer is: the local community residents, taxpayers, voters, community members, and businesses within the municipality. When we talk about local government interests, many of us talk about voters, taxpayers and residents, and community members and use these terms interchangeably. However, these are not necessarily the same people. Voters are those eligible to vote in municipal elections. We will learn later in the course that voters must be Canadian citizens, 18 years of age or older, and own property or live in the municipality. Municipal taxpayers are property owners they own property and pay property tax. These property owners may or may not live in the municipality and they may not be eligible to vote (for example, if they aren t Canadian citizens). Community members or residents includes anyone who lives within the municipality international students, recent immigrants, non-citizens, transients, etc. Community members may rent rather than own property. As you can see, each term has a different meaning and includes different people and interests; we will need to be careful to use the right terms. The role of municipalities is to provide good government and act in the best interests of the residents. But what does that really mean? Should councillors represent the majority view of their community members or should councillors do what they believe is best for the community? This discussion connects to the role of municipal councillors (that we will explore later), whether they play a delegate or trustee role. How do municipalities balance multiple conflicting interests? Rarely are all community members and businesses in agreement about an issue if the role of municipal decision makers is to act in the best interests of the majority (a delegate role), the challenge clearly is to identify and define that majority. Doesn t this mean that underrepresented, smaller groups will be marginalized? In addition, there is a need to balance business and residential interests and those of the taxpaying residents with others who do not own land or pay property tax directly. Similarly, how do municipalities balance current needs versus planning and working for the future? Should they vote for a short-term project that is supported by the local community or a longer-term project that will have greater but longer-term benefits? Municipalities also have to decide between purely local interests and larger regional or perhaps national interests. Many environmental issues have spillover effects on other areas. Should a municipality pursue its interests without considering the impact on others or on the broader environment? Why We Need to Study Local Government First, because it is interesting. We identify with some of the issues, we may know some of the people involved, and the political trade-offs are easier to understand. Local government directly affects our community. As well, studying local government helps us: make better, more informed decisions about political leadership in municipal elections; understand how decisions are made local governmental politics provide insight on power, influence, and the broader political system and on the role and positioning of municipalities within the provincial and national decision-making systems; reflect on the historical evolution of local government and perhaps provide a window on the future; understand where and how money is spent and services are delivered; contribute input as well as advocate for change and hold local decision makers accountable for their decisions; and connect residents in the municipality to one another and to the local level of government, which in turn strengthens the communities and their democratic foundations. This module provided an introduction to local government in Canada and set the foundation for the remainder of the course. It provided some important definitions local government, municipalities, and civil society and reviewed the structure of government in Canada. While municipalities are a key element of Canadian government, they are not formally recognized in the Canadian Constitution. This module concluded with a discussion of why local government is important and why it is important that you study it. Federalism is understood to be a political system in which the powers of the state are formally divided between central and regional (sub-national or provincial) governments : Click to see the results of the 2 Ontario survey In Canada, the constitutional framework lays out the division of power or jurisdictions among the multiple legislatures. In Canada, federal and provincial governments are organized into three branches the legislature, executive, and judiciary. Government is the group of representatives elected to a defined, formal institution with authority to govern a community or area. Governance is a broader term that refers to the processes of governing and relationships between the formal institutions of government and civil society. Local government is the lowest level of elected government in Canada and is also referred to as The Municipal Corporations Act, 1849, or Baldwin Act, is generally recognized as the foundation of local government as we know it today. In Canada, municipalities are institutions of provinces territories. Municipal roles and jurisdiction are defined in provincial legislation and consist mainly of service provision and political representation. Pause and Reflect Take some time to reflect on your understanding of the structure of government in Canada. What is distinctive about local government compared with the federal, provincial, and territorial governments? Unlike the federal, provincial, and territorial governments, local government and municipalities are not recognized as a level of government in the Constitution. They are often referred to as creatures of the province because provinces and territories have the sole responsibility to establish, restructure, or eliminate local government. Municipalities and other forms of local government are corporations established by provinces and territories with a responsibility to govern, but unlike the federal, provincial, and territorial levels, they are not formal levels of government. Municipalities and other forms of local government don t have three separate branches; they combine the legislative and executive functions in their elected councils, and unlike the federal, provincial, and territorial governments, they don t have a judicial role. : After reflecting on the question, click here to see some possible answers. Local government employs more staff and spends more than the federal, provincial, or territorial levels. This is because municipalities and their local agencies deliver a broad range of services. Objectives and Highlights To introduce the structure and operation of government at all levels. To illustrate the varied and valuable services provided by government. To develop your personal government directory. While there are many possible causes of the widespread public disillusionment with government, it seems clear that two reasons are that: (1) citizens aren't sure which level of government is responsible for what, and (2) even if they find the right level of government, they don't know whom to hold accountable or where to pursue their concern. They do, however, often feel that they are over-governed, a sentiment that may arise from the fact that most Canadians are under the jurisdiction of at least three levels of government, and often four. These are: 1. The national or federal government. 2. A provincial or territorial government, such as the government of Manitoba or the government of the Northwest Territories. 3. A municipal government, such as a village, town, city, or township. (In addition, there may be an upper tier municipal government, such as a county, regional, or district government, found mainly in Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia.) A good starting point is a list of names and phone numbers, such as the one you can compile using the Guide to Government Directory 2 A Citizen's Guide to Government provided at the end of this chapter. Once completed, it will provide you with a convenient checklist of contacts for your future interaction with government. Also in this chapter is a whimsical description of A Day in the Life of college student Frank N. Earnest, whose adventures serve to illustrate many of the important services and programs provided by the various levels of government in Canada. We begin with a brief overview of the general structure of government found at the federal, provincial, and local levels in Canada. Knowing which level of government looks after what is quite a challenge, especially when so many responsibilities are shared among two or more levels. Later chapters will shed more light on who does what, why responsibilities have become so intertwined, and what the implications are of efforts to disentangle responsibilities in recent years. This is the first of several chapters (see also Chapters 5 and 6) examining the organization and functioning of government at all levels. The Federal Government It is customary to discuss the organization of the federal (and provincial) government in terms of two separate branches, executive and legislative, and how they are interrelated - as depicted in Figure 2.1 on the next page. Most texts also identify a third branch, the judiciary or court system, about which more will be said in Chapter 7 of this Guide. For most Canadians, their main personal interaction with the federal government occurs approximately every four yearsl when they have an opportunity to elect from their riding one member of Parliament to the House of Commons. The Commons consists of 308 members elected from 308 geographic areas into which Canada is divided. These members are chosen to represent and make decisions 1 The maximum term for a Parliament is five years (except for a possible extension during an extreme emergency such as wartime), but the party in power usually calls an election toward the end of the fourth year. The timing depends on the party's assessment of when it is most likely to get re-elected. Chapter 2. What Are Our Many Governments? 23 on behalf of the Canadian population. This arrangement for representa- tive government is found in virtually every democratic governing structure. As will be seen, it is present in the election of legislative assemblies at the provincial level and of councils at the municipal level. It is also found in the election of student unions or student councils in colleges and universities. Fi ure 2.1 Government of Canada Executive Branch Legislative Branch Commons elected by people of Canada Besides its representative role, the House of Commons has two other key roles: (1) to pass laws, in the form of acts or statutes, for the governing of Canada, and (2) to act as a \"watchdog\" keeping an eye on the Cabinet and the civil service. The watchdog role is mainly carried out by the opposition members in the Commons, since members of the governing party are expected to support their Cabinet, not to criticize it. While the House of Commons receives most of the media and public attention, Canada's Parliament has two Houses. In this bicameral legislature, the Senate is the upper chamber. It shares the law making role of the Commons and must also give its approval before a bill can become a law. In addition, it plays a kind of watchdog role by giving \"sober second thought\" to actions taken by the Commons. This mature reflection was supposed to come from the appointment of leading Canadians from all walks of life, who would bring experience and sound judgment to the task. To be appointed, Senators must be at least 30 years of age, and they hold office until age 75. However, an appointed Senate 2 A Citizen's Guide to Government gradually lost legitimacy as notions of democracy and accountability took hold over the past century. Turning to the executive branch, the Governor General represents the Queen in Canada, reflecting the fact that Canada is a constitutional monarchy. The Governor General is appointed by the Queen (but on the advice of the Canadian Prime Minister), to act on her behalf when she is not in Canada. The Queen is the Head of State, ! whereas the Prime Minister is the head of government. These governing arrangements distinguish Canada from a republic like the United States, in which there isn't a separate Head of State different from the President. The Governor General has many official duties, in Canada and abroad. A number of the duties are automatic and simply involve the Governor General carrying out the \"advice\" given by the Prime Minister. This is true, for example, of the appointment of Cabinet ministers. Many of the duties are social and ceremonial in nature and could presumably be carried out by the Prime Minister, as they are by the President or other Head of State in countries that are republics. But the Prime Minister is a partisan, political figure, less suited to representing the country as a whole and is sufficiently burdened with other duties. For these reasons, there is much to be said for having a separate Head of State. Moreover, there are a limited number of discretionary powers vested in the Queen and Governor General that are rarely required but can be important in the operation of our system of government. These discretionary duties are explored in Chapter 5, but they help to make the position of Governor General more valuable and relevant than is commonly appreciated. That later chapter will also consider the merits of recent suggestions that the monarchy should be abolished in Canada. The key members of the executive branch are the Prime Minister and Cabinet. While the government of Canada consists of the various elements of governing machinery outlined in Figure 2.1, when people refer to \"The Government,\" they are usually thinking of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, which underlines the central position that they hold. The main responsibilities of the Cabinet include: (1) developing p-olicies to deal with the issues facing the country, (2) introducing bills to carry through these policies into law, and (3) supervising the civil servants who apply these policies and administer the laws on a day to day basis. Given the central importance of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, it is perhaps surprising that they are not directly elected by the Canadian people - although it can be said that they are indirectly chosen. This is true in the sense that by voting for the candidate of a particular party, we are helping to elect members of that party to the Commons. Normally, Chapter 2. VVhat Are Our Many Governments? 25 the party that elects the most members is deemed to have won the election. The leader of that party will become the Prime Minister of Canada and a number of other victorious candidates from that party will be chosen by the Prime Minister to serve as ministers in the federal Cabinet and to share in the running of the government. The principle of responsible government holds that the Cabinet is responsible to the House of Commons (from which its members come) and can only stay in office so long as it is supported by a majority of the members of the Commons. However, when a majority of the members of the Commons belongs to the same party as the members of the Cabinet, as is usually the case, this principle ceases to have much practical value. In such a situation, the governing party can almost always count on sufficient support in the assembly when required, and will continue to govern until the Prime Minister decides that the time is right to call an election - before the maximum five year tenn draws to a close. The Cabinet readily finds support when a majority of the members of the Commons belongs to the same party. The actual day to day work of the government of Canada is carried out by full time employees who are known as the civil service or public service. The majority of these employees work for government departments (like Agriculture, Fisheries, Health, Environment, Revenue, and Transport), and each department is headed by a minister of the Cabinet. Through this structure, the appointed civil servants are answerable to the Canadian people through elected politicians in the Cabinet. Through the long-standing principle of ministerial responsibility, ministers are held accountable for the perfonnance of the civil servants within their departments. Fi ure 2.2 Ministerial Res 2 A Citizen's Guide to Government The Provincial and Territorial Governments Canada is a federation. A federation is a system in which the functions of government are divided between two or more levels: a national government and provinces or states. In Canada's case, the federation is made up of one national government, ten provincial governments, and three territorial governments - the Yukon, the Northwest Territories, and the recently created territory ofNunavut, which came into existence on April I, 1999. The latter's small population of 25 000, 85 of whom are Inuit, is scattered across a vast area of the Eastern Arctic, an area roughly twice as large as Ontario. The Government of the Provinces If you understood the structure of the government of Canada, the governing arrangements at the provincial level are much the same, as is evident in Figure 2.3. Fi ure 2.3 The Government of a Province Executive Bra nch Legislative Branch Assembly elected by people of province The public's main participation is again through electing a representative body, in this case called the Legislative Assembly (or National Assembly in the case of Quebec). The number of members varies by province and ranges from a high of 125 in Quebec to only 27 members in Prince Edward Island. All provincial legislatures are Chapter 2. What Are Our Many Governments? 27 unicameral; there aren't any upper chambers like the Senate found at the national level. The Legislative Assembly has the same responsibilities as the House of Commons: to represent the people, to pass laws, and to act as a watchdog. The party winning the most seats in the Assembly makes up \"The Government,\" consisting of the Premier and Cabinet. The Cabinet is responsible to the Assembly and must have the support of its members; but here again, party loyalty usually ensures that support. The Cabinet has the same key roles as its federal counterpart: to develop policies, introduce laws, and supervise the administration of those laws. The day to day running of the government is again carried out by civil servants, mostly organized in departments headed by Ministers who sit in the Cabinet. The Lieutenant Governor is the official head of the provincial government (representing the Queen). He or she is appointed by the Queen on the advice of the federal government, which really means appointment by the Prime Minister. The roles of the Governor General also apply to the Lieutenant Governor. In addition, one of the traditional roles of the office was to act as an agent of the federal level in \"keeping an eye on\" provincial actions that might be contrary to the national interest. Given the strength of provincial governments today, however, any intervention of this sort by a Lieutenant Governor would not be tolerated. Overall, the government of a province operates on the same principles of representative and responsible government, and has much the same governing machinery - except that: It has a Legislative Assembly instead of a House of Commons. It doesn't have any second chamber like the Senate. It has a Lieutenant Governor instead of a Governor General. The members of the legislative assemblies are known as MLAs, with three exceptions. Ontario's members are officially known as MPPs or members of provincial Parliament, a presumptious affectation since there is only one Parliamen

They are correctly included under the general definition of \"local government.\" Agencies, boards, and commissions receive much less attention than municipalities in this text. While decisions made by these organizations can often greatly impact local government, ABCs are more a form of decentral- ized provincial and territorial administration than a vehicle through which local residents make decisions about the communities in which they live. In other words, ABCs provide an avenue for provincial and territorial govern- ments to deliver top-down policies, where municipal governments offer an opportunity for a more bottom-up, organic policy generation. LocAL GovERNANCE, MuLTILEVEL GovERNMENT, AND MuLTILEVEL GovERNANCE It is worth clarifying a few more terms before proceeding. For example, some use the term \"local governance\" when talking about particular types of local decision making. 8 Numbered \"2\" in Figure 1.1, \"local governance\" moves beyond the idea of municipal governments and ABCs making local government decisions to describe particular local decision- making scenarios involving municipal governments, ABCs, and civil society groups. The latter includes organizations such' as registered chari- ties, neighbourhood associations, faith-based organizations, women's organizations, professional associations, trade unions, self-help groups, social movements, business associations, and advocacy groups. \"Local government\" describes collaborative arrangements only between officials in local institutions with formal powers derived from the Constitution, while \"local governance\" defines scenarios where these local officials col- laborate with civil society groups with less or even no formal authority. Moving further along this path, arrangements between municipal and provincial government officials, municipal and federal government officials, or municipal and provincial and federal government officials are called \"multilevel government\" (numbered \"3\" in Figure 1.1). \"Mul- tilevel governance\" (numbered as \"4\" in Figure 1.1) is a situation when municipal governments and one or both senior levels of governments and civil society groups form cooperative agreements to work on local issues. 9 Though these terms occasionally come up in this text, you are likely to encounter them the more you read about local government. 8 For example, see Peter John, Local Governance in Western Europe, London: Sage, 2001. 9 This term originated in Europe and first appeared in Liesbet Hooghe and Gary Marks, Multi-Level Governance and European Integration, Lanham, MD: Rowman and Littlefield Publishers, 2001. The Promise of Local Government 9 The Role of Municipal Government The previous section described municipal governments as the key local govern- ment institutions. This section discusses the two main municipal government roles. On one hand, municipal governments are created by provinces and territories to deliver a wide range of necessary services, programs, facilities, and regulations to local residents. On the other hand, local residents expect elected municipal governments to express the will of the local community- even if what the community wants falls outside the authority of the municipal government to deliver or directly contradicts senior government policy. The growing scope of municipal government responsibility and pressures of living in a highly complex modern age often cause these two main roles to clash, but in combination they often offer the best local service provision approach. Big cities are also working on alternative fuel and energy technology as well as advanced transit systems, and are competing on the world stage to host the Olympics, the Pan-American Games, the Common- wealth Games and World Expositions. MUNICIPALITIES AS DEMOCRATIC GOVERNMENTS As valuable as it is to deliver all these services for provincial and territorial governments, many argue the core purpose of a municipal government is to provide a mechanism for local people to express, debate, and resolve local issues and concerns. To these local democrats, municipal govern- ments perform a vital political role and provide local citizens opportuni- ties to choose representatives who will make decisions reflecting-or at least addressing-community views and concerns. From this perspective, the municipality is an extension of the community and depicts the com- munity governing itself. 1 The democratic role of municipalities has been emphasized by various 19th century scholars such as John Stuart Mill and Alexis de Toc- quevilleY To Mill, municipal governments constitute a training ground where elected representatives learn how to govern before going on to serve at a more senior level of government and local citizens learn to exercise their democratic rights in the context of relatively simple-to- understand issues. Others view the democratic role of municipal govern- ments in a much more fundamental light, agreeing with de Tocqueville's sentiments that \"... municipal institutions constitute the strength of free nations .... A nation may establish a free government, but without municipal institutions it cannot have the spirit of liberty.\" 1 No better expression of this latter sentiment can be found in Canada than in the famous Durham Report. Sent in the 1830s by the British Government to investigate a series of rebellions in what was then Upper and Lower Canada, Lord Durham was struck by the lack of municipal institutions in the colonies, especially in the rural areas still governed by unelected Courts of Quarter Sessions.
