The role of participation in global world cities Maureen M. Donaghy INTRODUCTION Participation in organized groups is often difficult, sometimes boring, and always time con- suming. Voting can also be unappealing, particularly if none of the candidates represents an ideal choice. But politics cannot be transparent, responsive, or accountable to citizens without public participation. This is what we as scholars, activists, and advocates believe to be true, but research on public participation of various forms and in different contexts over the past few decades has sought to provide evidence as to when and how participation matters in public policy making, electoral politics, and neighborhood development. In the urban context these questions are critical as cities are the sites of protest, advocacy, community organizing, and electoral contestation. Scholars, along with government officials, practitioners, and activists, need answers to questions about participation to guide public policy making and institutional design in the modern democratic city. This brief chapter, then, examines what I hold as one of the most central questions for urban politics: When does citizen participation matter? As the chapter will discuss, questions of impact often center on who participates in political activities, why these individuals and groups choose to engage with the state, and how they ultimately make demands or enact change, from the neighborhood to the global level. Over the past several decades, the clash between capitalism and democracy across all these levels has become clearer along with questions of identity, inequality, and who decides the future direction of cities. Citizens come into conflict with developers and governments are meant to mediate claims to urban space. The extent to which citizens particularly those traditionally marginalized from politics can influence government decisions in the face of pressure to generate profits and public revenues often guides central debates in research on participation in urban politics. But in the last two decades scholars increasingly rely on the principles of the right to the city as envisioned by Henri Lefebvre in the 1960s to measure the extent to which cities reflect the desires of residents rather than a small segment of elites. Building on the work of Lefebvre, Purcell argues for a conception of democracy as a tendential project in which people continually increase their desire to manage their affairs themselves . In the urban context this means that people seek to manage the production of urban space on their own terms. In addressing when participation matters, then, the impact may be defined by the extent to which people, rather than governments or corporations, hold power in deciding the tangible and intangible characteristics of cities that shape their everyday lives. But what does this participation look like? In defining democratic norms scholars gen- erally argue that those affected by official decisions should have the right to participate in making them, or at least having their voices heard at some point in the policy-making process. Participation enables transparency in that public officials have to defend their positions, responsiveness in that those most affected must be involved in order to get the policies right, and accountability when officials must report results of policy implementation. But though Handbook of Urban Politics and Policy, edited by Ronald K. Vogel, Edward Elgar Publishing Limited, 2024. ProQuest Ebook Central, Created from torontomu on 2025-01-15 . Copyright 2024. Edward Elgar Publishing Limited. All rights reserved. The role of participation in global world cities 287 we might now see participation as necessary in municipal governance this hasn t always been the case. The idea that citizens might be involved in planning only came about in the 1950s and 1960s when problems with top-down planning became apparent within slum clearance and urban renewal programs. Public officials at the time had not realized the problems these programs would cause to residents. In response, the 1960s War on Poverty programs required the maximum feasible participation of the poor in antipoverty programs. Today, almost all federally funded urban programs in the United States now have this requirement, formally institutionalizing the norm of citizen participation with the goal of incorporating the most vulnerable and often invisible individuals into decision making. But the form that citizen participation takes is certainly not static. Though participa- tion has become more institutionalized in global cities, in the past decade new forms of mobilization around issues of gentrification and displacement as well as race, migration, education, and public safety have renewed interest in research on what leads individuals to join collective movements, how these movements seek change, and what the outcomes of various claims-making strategies may be. As we move forward with research on participation, increasingly understanding when citizens influence the democratic process is key to innova- tions in institutional design and ensuring urban policies and programs respond to the needs of residents. The remainder of this chapter seeks to explore the threads of these arguments further, concluding with what we know about when citizen participation matters for determining the purpose and use of cities as well as directions for future research. WHAT IS PARTICIPATION? To understand when participation matters, of course we must first start with defining the vague independent variable of participation and how it has evolved over time. In global cities, participatory practices generally include: voting, running for office, engaging in open forums, taking part in street protests, debating on social media, contacting public officials, providing testimony, and writing letters, among numerous other possibilities. Dahl argued for the primacy of public contestation and participation as the bedrock of democratic polyarchy. Participation, in his view, was primarily defined by engagement with the electoral process through party formation, voting, and campaigning, and he argued that the opportunity for civic engagement was necessary to mediate conflicting interests in democracy, concepts that we mostly now take for granted. Verba and Nie then defined participation as behavior meant to influence the actions of government officials and policy-making decisions, broad- ening the concept from the electoral process to other types of lobbying and advocacy. Since then, other authors have found this definition too narrow, particularly outside of the United States context. For example, examining political events in five Western democracies, Barnes and Kaase , include all activities meant to directly or indirectly influence the political system, specifically incorporating protest and violent activities and not just elections or direct claims-making of the state. In the context of social movements, Sidney Tarrow framed participation in terms of contentious vs. cooperative activities, either meant to disrupt the status quo or work with public officials to achieve demands. More recently comparative urban scholars have included the means of influence, in which advocates seek power directly through formal institutions or Handbook of Urban Politics and Policy, edited by Ronald K. Vogel, Edward Elgar Publishing Limited, 2024. ProQuest Ebook Central, Created from torontomu on 2025-01-15 . Copyright 2024. Edward Elgar Publishing Limited. All rights reserved. 2 Handbook of urban politics and policy mediated through efforts to influence voting and policy making from the outside . Eleonora Pasotti defines experiential tools embedded in cultural practices as repertoires of collective action, particularly in bringing attention to issues such as displace- ment and gentrification in cities worldwide. These types of performative activities often go hand in hand with voting and other traditional forms of protest to enable more voices to be heard, particularly from marginalized communities. Communities, themselves, also define what participation means to them. In the 1960s, Saul Alinsky urged urban residents to engage in community organizing, building on a community s power resources and assets to empower residents to bring about positive change. Since then, community organizations in the United States have largely turned away from protest towards more cooperative tactics, forming partnerships with public agencies to improve service deliv- ery and other conditions in neighborhoods. Community development corporations , which are neighborhood-based-non-profits, work with public and private entities to secure investments in low-income communities, and have had great success in generating and pre- serving affordable housing, health clinics, food banks, and other necessities. Working within these types of organizations may also be seen as a form of political participation in cities. In fact, Ostrom emphasized that communities have largely already developed ways of dealing with the challenges they face, and rather than imposing solutions from above the state should empower residents to further take charge. She developed the concept of co-production, in which citizens participate directly in the design and delivery of public services. Research by scholars such as Bovaird continues to emphasize the benefits of long-term relationships between public service users, community groups, and public sector bureaucrats through the process of co-production. Further, in the past two decades, research on participation has also shifted to understand the role of social media and new forms of participatory governance institutions as political partic- ipation. Social media serves as a platform for organizing in-person gatherings and events, but as Castells argues, it is also a mechanism for inciting participation through engaging with users emotions. Research continues to explore for whom social media influences par- ticipation and the impact of social media use on electoral choices, participation in advocacy campaigns, and other forms of individual and collective action. Continuing to calculate the balance between citizens and the state, the study of participation in governance arrangements has also evolved in the recent past. From public management literature, participation includes a broad range of governance activities, defined by Torfing . as the complex process through which a plurality of actors with diverging interests interact in order to formulate, promote and achieve common objectives by means of mobilizing, exchanging and deploying a range of ideas, rules and resources. Participation in governance processes is increasingly formalized in cities around the world. Literature on par- ticipatory governance institutions has proliferated over the last two decades, particularly since the installation of a participatory budgeting process in Porto Alegre, Brazil, which has served as a model for thousands of other cities. Scholars have sought to understand how par- ticipatory processes evolve, who participates, and how practices transfer to different contexts. Since the 1960s, our knowledge and understanding of what constitutes political partici- pation in cities has only grown as has our definition. The multitude of activities possible as forms of urban participation provides endless opportunities for research. But scholars must also be mindful to explicitly define participation in the urban context relevant to our places of study to clarify its meaning and impact for the population. If we want to know when citizen Handbook of Urban Politics and Policy, edited by Ronald K. Vogel, Edward Elgar Publishing Limited, 2024. ProQuest Ebook Central, Created from torontomu on 2025-01-15 . The role of participation in global world cities 289 participation matters for shaping our cities, how we define participation must clearly move beyond electoral politics and traditional forms of protest to everyday forms of claims-making, cooperation, autonomous solutions, social networking, and shared governance. From the broadening definition of participation, we see the myriad ways that individuals and groups act, reinforcing the notion that there is no one set of actions that matters for shaping the lives of residents within cities. WHO PARTICIPATES? Though we see that citizen participation never takes just one form in any context, who par- ticipates should influence the voices that rise to the top of policy and decision making. For decades research and evidence as to who participates in politics in cities often focused on socioeconomic and demographic characteristics. From the 1960s questions of the relationship between income, education, and participation took priority. For example, Verba, Schlozman, and Brady found that lower-income and less educated citizens in the U.S. participated in politics less than those who were wealthier and more educated. Men (especially white men) have been more likely to participate in direct contact and collective action than women (Mansbridge 1983; Kittilson 2016). The elderly have higher levels of participation (Campbell 2003; Schlozman, Verba, and Brady 2012) as do people who have lived in their homes longer (Kang and Kwak 2003; Gay 2012) and own their homes . Wealthier citizens are also more likely to get involved in required participatory processes in the U.S. and there is evi- dence of voluntary participatory processes being dominated by middle- and upper-class urban residents in NYC , Minneapolis , and Los Angeles . All of these findings suggest a bias in conflict with the goal of enabling diverse voices in politics and policy making. Further, in recent challenges to spatial and resource distribution for housing in cities, researchers have found similar profiles for those who get involved in local politics. For example, Einstein, Palmer, and Glick compare individuals participating in planning and zoning board meetings on housing development to voter files in cities in Massachusetts, finding that people who are older, male, longtime residents, voters in local elections, and homeowners are significantly more likely to participate in these meetings. This group is also more likely than the general population to oppose new housing construction, leading to the conclusion that who participates in local politics has significant policy implications for development. From the studies above we see that who participates matters for shaping the city. And research on inclusivity in cities shows that neighborhood participation is key to providing voice to underrepresented groups and enhancing democracy (Berry, Portney, and Thomson 1993; Fung 2006; Michaels and de Graaf 2010; Stone and Stoker 2015). What we need is more research on how to ensure these groups do in fact get involved and that we design processes to meet diverse needs and interests in order to correct imbalances in power and representation. In terms of increasing diversity in who votes, research has shown mixed effects on specific interventions, such as early voting and initiatives to ease the burden of registration. Berinsky actually finds that these reforms are associated with an increase in socioeconomic ine- qualities in turnout. Burden and Neiheisel , however, finds that election day registration increases overall turnout, but early voting can decrease turnout without other reforms. So what does motivate urban residents to get involved in politics? Digging deeper, scholars have discovered further trends about why individuals choose to participate in political activ- ities. For example, economics and ideology often provide the motivation for mobilization around specific issues, such as financialization of housing and segregation of territory. Anger is also a powerful emotion associated with an increase in electoral participa- tion as are altruism and social identification associated with an increase in all types of political participation . Immigrants are also heavily involved in urban politics, often as opposed to formal and national politics, including partici- pation in local street life and engagement with the arts, often using media and communication technologies . Though Putnam blames declining social capital for lack of civic engagement by traditional means, he does find that citizens are increasingly likely to get involved in identity-based organizations, including non-profit advocacy groups. Individuals are also willing to get involved in political issues when they are likely to see a return on their investment of time and energy. This argument follows from the work of Olson , who found that where benefits to the individual are not so clear, people need selective incentives to participate in order to overcome the collective action problem. In some instances, however, though benefits may not be individualized, residents can see collective rewards. For example, in participatory budgeting processes in Brazil, Goldfrank found that people were more likely to continue to participate if they saw tangible results from their efforts, such as new sidewalks or streetlights in their neighborhoods. Further research identified similar effects in participatory budgeting processes in New York City . In a study of three Western European cities, Bologna, Stuttgart, and Zaragoza, Manes-Rossi . found that citizens were more likely to continue participating when they perceived their role as effec- tive in the co-production of outcomes. Still, other scholars have criticized the focus on community participation as the solution to urban conflicts and challenges of service delivery. David Harvey writes, One of the aspects of much contemporary debate about the urban which I find particularly striking is the tendency when faced with all sorts of difficulties again and again to reach into this bag called community , on the assumption that community is going to save us all. Community, endowed with salving powers, is perceived as capable of redeeming the mess which we are creating in our cities A lot of community construction projects are, in the end, a recipe for isolation. They isolate groups from the city as a whole. () Harvey recognizes that the community cannot be separated from the structure, logic, and institutions of the whole city, but when we rely on communities to solve local issues we often seem to forget this, leaving the individuals within a specific location responsible for the fate of their own development. Further, in global development literature, Cooke and Kothari make the case that participation represents a new tyranny in which the most powerful in communities often are the only voices to be heard, reinforcing existing dynamics. Additionally, they argue that local knowledge and decision-making processes are often overridden by outsiders who bring their own toolboxes to manage projects. In the U.S. context, marginalized groups also report what Sally Nuamah describes as a a type of mobilization fatigue that transpires when citizens engaged in policy processes are met with a lack of democratic transparency and responsive- Handbook of Urban Politics and Policy, edited by Ronald K. Assessing qualitative data from public meetings on school closures in low-income black neighborhoods, Nuamah finds negative perceptions of local government and collective participatory debt among partici- pants who feel they are used as tokens of representation rather than sincere partners. In sum, research has shown the basic difficulty of ensuring diverse and inclusive participa- tion of residents without over-burdening those who have the least time and resources to get involved, particularly when their involvement does not lead to meaningful input and progress in their communities and cities at large. Moving forward, there are plentiful opportunities for research on urban participation for the purpose of understanding why some residents do and do not participate over others and the resulting impact of these choices. We know that partici- pation matters for shaping the city when the loudest or wealthiest voices are heard. But when more diverse voices are involved in more genuine forms of policy making and deliberation with clear benefits for those who make the time and give their energy to engage, participation should be more likely to create the types of cities that meet the needs of broad populations. THE HOW OF PARTICIPATION Politics is defined by the contests between citizens for power. ipation, then, has primarily focused on how non-elites or those without formal powers of representation are able to gain influence for political and policy outcomes. But participation writ-large is often taken for granted as having an influence on outcomes without careful examination. As Burton states, for something that is held to be so important and to deliver a myriad of benefits, we know little of the extent to which the benefits of public participation are in fact delivered or of the balance of these benefits with any costs. In recent years, however, this has begun to change as urban scholars, in particular, seek to understand when and how individual and collective actions matter. Three areas in which scholarship has focused include, the role of coalitions, the rules of participatory processes, and the strategies of organizations to achieve their goals. COALITIONS Dahl argued that urban political power, as opposed to national, is fragmented and involves many different people from different backgrounds in decision making. But, even if this were true, scholars have been skeptical about the potential for citizen impact. Molotch (1976, 1979) and Logan and Molotch argued that growth machines, made up of pro-growth coalitions, make decisions about land use, public expenditures, and urban social life. These growth machines include public officials, the media, and union leadership to support projects of accumulation. The quest for profits and revenues limits the ability of outsiders, including non-elite citizens, to affect power over urban decision making. Clarence Stone reinforced the idea that citizens have limited impact through his study of Atlanta. He argued that coalitions develop between like-minded public, private, and civil society actors. Because the demands of low-income neighborhoods are not aligned with the quest for revenues and profits, citizen groups may make incremental progress but will never overcome the coalition of monied interests. In the era of globalization, Saskia Sassen added that Handbook of Urban Politics and Policy, edited by Ronald K. Vogel, Edward Elgar Publishing Limited, 2024. ProQuest Ebook Central, Created from torontomu on 2025-01-15 . Copyright 2024. Edward Elgar Publishing Limited. All rights reserved. 2 Handbook of urban politics and policy global competition reinforces the power of elites to shape the policy agenda and outcomes. Castells also contended that the ability of transnational networks to wield power in cities desperate for revenues negates the needs and desires of urban residents. But in truth, evidence over the last two decades demonstrates that there is not uniformity across cities in how citizens impact politics and policies. We see many instances in which growth coalitions appear to win over neighborhood coalitions, but we also see instances in which groups of citizens can change the direction of policy outcomes. Jones-Correa and Wong describe the success of housing groups in NYC, labor rights in LA, and education groups in Detroit, and demonstrate the importance of resource mobilization and sustained agendas for long-term impact. Stone, himself, along with his co-authors also maintains that in the current era the lines between actors are no longer as rigid as when he wrote in the late 1980s. New framing of issues around equity and sustainability for long-term growth means greater recognition of the importance of investments in communities and neighborhoods and not just downtowns and corporations. In addition, Stone and Stoker relate the willing- ness of community organizations to bargain instead of protesting as a means to compromise and multi-faceted solutions. Moderation on all sides of urban development conflicts enables citizen groups to have greater impact on policies than in the past. In addition, scholars charge that coalitional theories of development do not necessarily apply when we look past the primary cities of the U.S. and Europe. Fox contends that both the growth machine approach and regime theory assume strong independence of municipal governments, which is not always the case, particularly in developing countries with a legacy of colonial governance . Further, writing about African cities, LeBas argues that although there is variation, party institutionalization does not exist in a similar way to the two-party system in the U.S. Without a strong party system, fractionalization may make coa- litions for development more precarious. Finally, the intentions of activists may vary across contexts. As Walton finds, some actors may display a preference for clientelism when benefits are worth loyalty, thereby prioritizing short-term gains over long-term advocacy objectives. This line of research reminds us that not all interests are as we presume, and local norms cannot be ignored in our analyses of outcomes. INSTITUTIONAL DESIGN IN PARTICIPATORY PROCESSES Participatory processes inherently take away power from public officials and entrenched interests, both of which may stymie the process by not really giving meaningful opportuni- ties for citizens to impact outcomes. Since the late 1960s questions regarding the design of participatory processes and later the institutional rules and norms of participatory institutions pose fruitful research avenues across political science, urban planning, public policy, public management, and development scholars. In 1969, Sherry Arnstein developed A Ladder of Citizen Participation, which sought to characterize different types of participatory processes and their resulting impact. At a time when municipal governance sits at the intersection of global and local, public and private actors, Arnstein provides a typology for how citizens are to participate to increase representa- tion of their interests and elicit accountability. At the bottom of the ladder, manipulation, a contrived or fake attempt to bring in citizens voices, and therapy, trying to change the people involved and not the program, are both akin to non-participation. These are the outcomes of Handbook of Urban Politics and Policy, edited by Ronald K. Vogel, Edward Elgar Publishing Limited, 2024. ProQuest Ebook Central, Created from torontomu on 2025-01-15 . Copyright 2024. Edward Elgar Publishing Limited. All rights reserved. The role of participation in global world cities 293 public officials giving lip-service to the idea of participation without genuine interest or possi- bly even with mal-intent. In the middle, participatory processes that inform, consult, or placate offer a degree of tokenism, but without giving citizens significant decision-making power. At the top of the ladder, partnership, delegated power, and citizen control indicate the highest levels of community impact on planning and policy-making outcomes. While we see many examples of partnerships between public, private, and non-profit entities across cities, critics argue that citizen control can actually promote inefficient and balkanized public services with many questions arising over which groups deserve this power. In any case, the ladder was pivotal for demonstrating that not all participatory processes equally generate citizen impact and provided a typology for future researchers to label the types of processes they examined and measure the resulting impact. Comparative scholars have also conducted research on the implementation of participatory institutions, particularly for budgeting, in cities around the world. Meant to enable community members to directly decide spending priorities, participatory budgeting has traveled to over 1500 cities worldwide . The problem, according to Baiocchi and Ganuza is that the institutional innovations of the first instances of PB in Brazil have not translated to these processes around the world, often failing to ensure the participation of the most marginalized groups as originally intended. Wampler . argue that PB has been transferred to other contexts without the basic element of empowered decision making. Though Touchton and Wampler find that in Brazil PB is associated with improvements in the well-being of residents, these benefits are not guaranteed without dedicated public officials and rules that enable decision-making power of citizens. In fact, across cities in the U.S. and Europe, research finds the collaboration across stake- holders is key. Pateman finds in the U.S. context that though many individuals are hesitant to get involved in participatory budgeting, collaboration between public adminis- trators and citizens, which varies considerably across contexts, makes it easier for citizens to feel welcome and like their voices matter. In European cities, Manes-Rossi . find that the municipality must commit to genuine two-way dialogue for PB to generate co-production. Outside of PB, these same principles apply to other participatory governance institutions, including municipal councils for housing across Brazil . Archon Fung and Erik Olin Wright also find that participatory institutions need rough equality of power among participants from the beginning to be mechanisms of empowered participatory governance . Once again, influence is not guaranteed through the formalization of participation, but rather the state must agree to share power with citizens to affect impact. STRATEGIES Lastly, scholars have asked what types of engagement are most successful in achieving aims. The choices made by individuals and organizations of citizens in terms of goals, tactics, targets, and the means of influence should matter for their impact. Some findings for best practices are clear. For example, Liao and Ma argue that citizen participation needs to be carefully planned, coordinated, and supported by strategic partners. Ianniello . find that to be successful organizations need the support of officials and an organizational structure with clear community representation. All rights reserved. 2 Handbook of urban politics and policy enhances citizens knowledge of the issues and constraints around solutions faced by various stakeholders. In addition, the ideology of collective movements shapes the strategies they pursue and their ensuing impact. Most recently urban movements have sprung up all over the world under the banner of the right to the city. Like discussed above, Henri Lefebvre first argued in the 1960s that all residents should have the collective right to shape the many aspects of their city . As traced by Peter Marcuse , Lefebvre argued that the call for the right to the city could manifest in different ways, from demands for inclusion in the benefits of the city to outright transformation of policies and institutions to address the needs of the most mar- ginalized in society. How collective actors interpret the right to the city matters for the strate- gies they use and the goals they want to achieve. For example, a more conservative approach to the right to the city might include the demand for more subsidized housing to low-income residents while a more radical approach might call for a wholesale change in the provision of government housing in which low-income residents, themselves, define solutions and manage a collective process of decision making and program implementation. Harvey calls for the accumulation of dispossession in which low-income communities claim ownership over land they may have lived on for years, negating the power of elites to control capital in the city. Along these lines, Eleonora Pasotti studied 29 cases of anti-development protests in aspiring global cities, explaining how and why mobilization occurs and then why it is or is not successful. She finds that experiential tools significantly motivate mobilization, especially when combined with protest legacies and broad networks but these strategies have the most impact when protestors have strong allies in city government and there is not a right-wing alignment between the mayors and executives at the state and federal levels. The ideological motivation for strategies is key to success, but only when combined with allies in govern- ment. Donaghy finds similar outcomes in the study of community organizations for housing across cities in the U.S. and Brazil in which a radical ideology combined with aligned governments in power created the best opportunities for impact on generating and preserving affordable housing for low-income residents. In sum, research to date has found a number of variables that influence how participation impacts policy making, institutions, and public programs. The role of coalitions while not a given still may be critical in any context for understanding the barriers and opportunities for the ability of citizens to succeed in eliciting benefits and services or determining the path of urban development. In addition, we know that all forms of participatory processes are not the same in terms of the powers given to residents and the potential influence they may have. The more responsibilities given to citizens in participatory processes over a concerted time frame, the more bonds of trust are formed on all sides. And in the end, the strategies of collective actors in terms of the goals and tactics they pursue, are both determined by their ideology and relationship with the state and determine the strength of their impact on urban development outcomes. CURRENT STATE AND FUTURE OF THE FIELD It may seem hyperbolic, but to understand the role of participation in shaping cities that meet the needs of citizens may very well mean the difference between life and death. Whether citizens have access to clean water, dignified housing, and quality education and are able to Handbook of Urban Politics and Policy, edited by Ronald K. Vogel, Edward Elgar Publishing Limited, 2024. ProQuest Ebook Central, Created from torontomu on 2025-01-15 . Copyright 2024. Edward Elgar Publishing Limited. All rights reserved. The role of participation in global world cities 295 mitigate and adapt to the impacts of climate change requires individuals and groups to demand more of cities, states, and national governments currently unable or unwilling to provide solu- tions. Because of these very real, imminent challenges facing cities the focus on local politics has only increased in recent decades. Trounstine argued that local politics has been marginalized as a subfield in previous decades. But apart from the ethical reasons for studying participation in cities, she cites three methodological factors that motivate increasing attention to the local and urban levels of study. First, there are a great number of political events happening at the local level from which to draw our cases. Second, cities offer methodological advantages in terms of diversity, variety, and number of cases, and third, cities generate very different questions than looking at the national level. In essence, we need to understand how and why cities are unique entities and the number of diverse cases provides a seemingly never-ending supply of events, institutions, policies, and populations from which to choose. Given the wealth of available data and the number of cities within and across national borders, the study of participation in urban politics is not constrained to one methodology. While many studies rely on survey and electoral data for quantitative analysis related to who participates in politics, scholars are also applying these methods to the study of protests, com- munity mobilization, and individual contact with representatives, among many other types of participation, assisted by data available online through social media, non-profit advocacy groups, and government agencies. Still, in-depth case studies of participation are often a pre- ferred method of scholars wishing to make causal inferences between activities and outcomes, and as noted above, more recently scholars have begun to look across cities that vary by soci- oeconomic characteristics for broader generalizations or idiosyncrasies in urban politics (for example, Pasotti 2020 and Donaghy 2018). This emphasis on understanding causal relationships between participation and outcomes fits within the approach of critical urban theory, which as Neil Brenner states, emphasizes the politically or ideologically mediated, socially contested and therefore malleable character of urban space that is, its continual construction as a site, medium, and outcome of his- torically specific relations of power . Critical urban theory takes on a somewhat normative position as to the goals of democracy and equality as it insists that another, more democratic, socially just, and sustainable form of urbanization is possible, even if such possi- bilities are currently being suppressed through dominant institutional arrangements, practices, and ideologies (Brenner 2012: 11). Brenner, Marcuse, and Mayer argue that the economic crisis of 2008 2009 intensi- fied unrest against capitalism across the globe and our goal now should be to understand how each city fits within the system of capital accumulation. Cities are the sites where conflicts over accumulation take place and research is needed to understand both the site-specific processes of urban restructuring as well as comparisons of how conflicts emerge and possibly resolve across cities. Along these lines, Brenner, Marcuse, and Mayer suggest research pro- jects to uncover: systematic injustices, exclusions, and marginalizations; the balance of social forces; and the lines of conflict. Recently, scholars have also argued for the application of American political development to urban politics, i.e. urban political development . Building on the approach of studying ideas, interests, and institutions over time, Weaver defines UPD as driven by intercurrent operation of multiple urban political orders, which are comprised of political coalitions, driven by overarching purposes (or ideas) that capture control of governing institu- Handbook of Urban Politics and Policy, edited by Ronald K. Vogel, Edward Elgar Publishing Limited, 2024. ProQuest Ebook Central, Created from torontomu on 2025-01-15 . Copyright 2024. Edward Elgar Publishing Limited. All rights reserved. 2 Handbook of urban politics and policy tions. To understand the direction of change within cities, then, we need to study the ideology or ideas that guide current actors and not just the economics of growth. Urban scholars may use the UPD framework to guide their narratives of how and when cities change over time given the ideas, interests, and institutions in place to either confine or motivate activities and impact. As urban research proceeds in the coming years, both critical urban theory and urban political development, among other approaches utilizing quantitative and qualitative methods will continue to intermingle and contribute to our understanding of the role of participation in cities. We can expect that comparative urbanism will examine how different cities are positioned within global economic and political dynamics, how various forms of governance interact to create openings for citizen influence, and how the formal and informal norms of cities create power and voice. Moving forward scholars need to recognize and study the diverse ways that urban residents participate in politics and why some means of participation appeal more to some groups than others. Post Covid-19, the study of the use of technology for interactive participation between citizens and government will likely also grow as will the question of how crises affect participation. Crises including displacement of people across borders, climate change, housing affordability, and disease epidemics threaten the very operation of urban governments and necessitate comprehensive solutions from citizens of all classes, ethnicities, races, ages, and genders. CONCLUSIONS How we define participation, who participates, and how citizen engagement is carried out all influence when citizen participation matters for shaping cities to meet the needs of residents now and into the future. Scholars have defined participation in numerous ways, and as we look beyond the cities of the U.S. and Western Europe, we continue to reevaluate from whose perspective we are labeling political participation and what those labels mean for how we consider who participates and the impact of their activities. In terms of who participates as we generally define the term, we know that those who are wealthier, white, and male tend to be more engaged in formal governmental processes, though as issues of gentrification, school violence, housing, and other local challenges impact marginalized communities and individuals, we see increasing activism among marginalized populations though scholars still need to work on understanding how participatory processes can work to engage diverse residents. Neither coalitions, nor participatory institutions, nor the strategies of urban-based organizations alone are the key to actions that make a difference to the direction of cities, but sharing power and cooperating across government and community actors in multiple ways can lead to change. At the end of the day, sitting through long meetings, standing in line to vote, marching in the hot sun or cold rain, have to matter or citizens will become less rather than more engaged. And in cities, whose voices are heard in the halls of power as well as how communities create change within their own spaces will shape the course of urban development. Scholars will need to work diligently to keep up with the changing relationships among actors to provide vital answers to when citizen participation matters. The adoption of open government by local governments in Canada: Obstacles and possibilities Anna Kopec Department of Political Science University of Toronto Byron Sheldrick Department of Political Science University of Guelph Abstract The purpose of this paper is to explore the extent to which dimensions of open government have been adopted by local governments in Canada. Local government structures are sometimes conceptualized as particularly well suited to democratic experimentation. Certainly, it has been the case that many governmental democratic reform initiatives have started at the local municipal level. Exploring open government at the local level provides us with insights into two questions. First, it helps us determine the extent to which open government has permeated beyond federal and provincial levels of government in Canada. Second, due to the challenges associated with open government, it allows us to identify and highlight such challenges. Keywords: open government; local government in Canada: Obstacles and possibilities Introduction Open government has a long history dating back to the 1950s. As a concept, it was originally linked to freedom of information debates and was seen a critical precondition of accountability (Parks 1957; Clarke and Francoli 2014; Yu and Robinson 2012). Open government, as such, had clear links to notions that democratic governments should not operate in secrecy, but rather that government information should be public information, and that decisions should be made transparently if there is to be accountability. This understanding of open government, while important, re- mained firmly rooted in a relatively traditional concept of liberal democracy. The concept of open government was given new life in 2008 with the election of Barak Obama as president of the United States . The launch of President Obama s Open Government Directive led to a revival of the concept and added new dimensions to the conceptualization of open government. In addition to traditional notions of access to information and decision-making transparency, open government became linked to concepts of citizen participation and the transformation of the relationship between state and citizen (Catlaw and Sandberg 2014; Pyrozhenko 2015). The concept of open government is also inextricably linked to the revolution in information technology and the rise of social media. The growth of new technological platforms for connecting and communicating with citizens has potentially transformed the nature of the democratic relationship between govern- ments and those they govern (O Reilly 2010; Francoli 2011; Mulgan 2014; Millard 2015; Sandoval-Almazon and Gil-Garcia 2016). These dimensions of open government raise the possibility of moving beyond traditional unders- tandings of liberal democracy towards a more radical democratization of state structures. Urban studies, in general, has not directly addressed the question of open government. Despite this, there are clear intersections between the study of open government and urban studies. Fundamentally, urban studies is inherently interdisciplinary, examining the urban environment, including social interactions, governance, political accountability, economics, and socio-legal dimensions. In short, urban studies inquires as to how people live in urban spaces. In so it employs techniques of political science, public administration, geography, sociology, criminology, economics, and law. The study of open government, in contrast, examines how governance is organized and structured. Its concern is with the development of transparent and participatory structures of decision-making, that enable and empower citizens to participate in the making of decisions that impact their lives. The concern of open government scholars is with both the creation of democratic processes, but also with information flows, and the developing capacity for decision-making, particularly through technology and social media. If we relate this to urban studies, we can see clear connections to those scholars who seek to examine the governance structure of local decision-making (Lucas 2017, Joy and Vogel 2017), but also to those who are interested in the development of smart cities, and the deployment of technology to both enhance urban life, and to ensure the economic competitiveness of cities (DeFilippis 1999; MacLeod 2011; Hoffman 2014). Similarly, the New Urbanism has developed an approach to urban planning which emphasizes holistic design and the creation of human scaled development that enhances the livability of urban spaces for all those who live in cities (see Charter of New Urbanism, sources what-new-urbanism). Open government is consistent with the principles of new urbanism, in that it seeks to enhance the political engagement and capacity of citizens. In a local context, it seeks to create human-scaled governance processes, so that design is not just an urban planning concept, but also a governance concept. The purpose of this paper is to explore the various dimensions of open government and determine the extent to which they have permeated local government in Canada. Local government structures are sometimes conceptualized as particularly well suited to democratic experimentation (Raven 2017; Caprotti and Cowley 2017; Kronsell and Mukhtar-Landgren 2018). Certainly, it has been the case that many governmental democratic reform initiatives have started at the local municipal level. Exploring open government at the local level provides us with insights into two questions. First, it helps us determine the extent to which open government has permeated beyond federal and provincial levels of government in Canada. Second, it allows us to examine variation in adoption at the local level and associated challenges. There has been much talk of open government at the federal and provincial levels. The federal government and eight of 10 provinces have made an explicit commitment to open government (Government of Ca- nada, Open Government. More specifically, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, PEI, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland and Labrador have all implemented open government ini- tiatives and have dedicated open government portals. Additionally, the government of the Northwest Territories has also endorsed open government principals. 7 CJUR 70ThThfi1 flff:2 flffiflffi Canadian Journal of Urban Research Revue canadienne de recherche urbaine The local level, however, is less frequently examined in relation to open government strategies in Canada. The adoption of open government principles by local governments is not without its challenges, and investigating the permeation of open government at the local level may highlight these challenges. Municipalities, for example, may lack the resources to pursue open government in a fulsome manner. The shear diversity of local government structures, therefore, may be an important factor. Large municipalities might have greater success in pursuing open government strategies, while smaller municipal governments may struggle. In other instances, local officials may consider themselves already well connected to their citizenry. This might also run counter to the implementation of open government principles, particularly in small municipalities. If everyone knows the mayor and councillors personally, the need to pursue elaborate strategies of citizen engagement may not be a high priority. In this context, open government may become redefined as simply the normal process of government operations, buttressed by de- mocratic elections. It may also be that some elements of open government may be easier for local governments to implement than others. By examining those local governments that have embraced open government, it allows us to get a better sense of what dimensions of open government are most popular and or easiest to implement, as well as what obstacles exist to the implementation and adoption of open government. The degree to which some of the radical potential of open government has been realized can then be assessed. Finally, this research serves an important purpose in understan- ding the value associated with the study of open government, as well as the limitation of such a project. This paper is divided into four sections. The first part provides an overview of the evolution of open govern- ment as a concept and the application of the term. The adoption of open government in the Canadian context will be specifically addressed. The second section of the paper outlines the methodological approach to the research and some of the limitations encountered. Finally, the results of our survey will be examined and discussed. In so, we emphasize the different open government strategies that have been pursued at the local level and also consider the limitations of local capacity to pursue open government. Finally, we conclude with a consideration of the implications of our findings and the potential for future research in this area. Open government as a concept Open government is an evolving concept. At one level, it is a strategy designed to transform information flows between the state and citizens, and by so allow citizens to interact with, impact, and reuse, that information. The result is a more engaged and active governance process. The growth of support for the correlation of good go- vernance with the cooperation of all stakeholders, including laypeople, has further supported the growth of open go- vernment initiatives. Cooperation and collaboration strengthens democracy with the creation of new government-ci- tizen relationships and networks that serve the needs of the community. Open government enhances governance and the quality of policymaking through greater transparency, collaboration and accountability (Misuraca and Viscusi 2014; Catlaw and Sanberg 2014; Scandoval-Almazon and Gil-Garcia 2016; Trivellator, Boselli and Cavenago 2014; Millard 2015). Open government, then, is a multilateral process that includes the elements of transparency, collaboration and participatory government. People and technologies are integrated into government action thereby serving the twin goals of enhancing participation and efficiency effectiveness. It creates opportunities for new forms of knowledge and insight with the use of external resources to achieve government goals. The goals of open government, however, are not always clear or well-defined; the term is subject to considerable theoretical ambiguity. As a concept, many scholars have noted its lack of definitional clarity and weak theoretical underpinnings (Lennon and Berg-Cross 2010; Clarke and Francoli 2014; Writz and Birkmeyer 2015). Clarke and Francoli have tried to overcome this by generating a detailed qualitative analysis of the themes included in seven national open government plans housed by the Open Government Partnership . The partnership is an international platform for sharing open government initiatives that was launched in 2011. Essentially, it operates as a repository and clearinghouse for open government projects. Its focus, however, is very much on national governmental plans. The partnership originally included eight countries, but has grown to over 70 countries, including Canada. Each government has an open government action plan which can be accessed through the Partnership website (Yu and Robinson 2011; Clarke and Francoli 2014; Harrison and Sayogo 2014). The OGP recommends that government plans should include the following core principles: transparency, citizen participation, accountability, and technology and innovation. Based on these values, Clarke and Francoli identified a further 14 themes that they used to analyze government plans housed with the OGP. These included: 7 CJUR 70ThThfi1 flff:2 flffiflffi 3e adoption of open government by local governments in Canada: Obstacles and possibilities Access to information; Accountability; Public participation; Open data; Reuse of government information and data; Drive economic growth promote innovation; Improve information management; Improve public services; Protect civil rights and privacy; Transparency; Alternative service delivery; Make government more efficient; Prevent corruption; Promote corporate accountability Clarke and Francoli s analysis found that, in general, more traditional understandings of open government, rooted in access to information, remained predominant in most plans, but with a concern for public participation added to the mix. In general, they found the four most common themes to be: Access to information Accountability Public participation Open data Open data is clearly related to the more traditional open government theme of access to information. It does, howe- ver, add an important technological dimension, and highlights the importance of new information technologies in the open government literature. Open data includes the creation of data repositories based on state collected and generated information that can be readily and freely accessed by citizens, corporations, and NGOs.These themes of data information are combined with themes of accountability and public participation. Opening up access to information, and generating new forms of information, is seen as critical to government ac- countability and transparency, and a step to empowering citizens to participate in governmental processes. Again, a technological dimension is added with the utilization of information technologies, including social media, to create accountability mechanisms and citizen participation. In many open government frameworks, these four themes are viewed as inextricably linked. Access to information and open data provide the tools for citizen engagement and participation, which in turn enhances accountability (see also Francoli 2011; Dawes and Helbig 2010; Lathrop and Ruma (Eds.) 2010). How far has open government travelled in Canada Given the commitment of the federal government to a formal open government plan, the question remains as to how far this has travelled from the federal level to provincial and local levels of government. The structure of the Cana- dian constitution, and in particular the division of powers in ss. 91 and 92, ensures that federal and provincial levels of government are largely autonomous. The federal government does not have the capacity to determine or dictate provincial policy in this area. However, given the widespread provincial endorsement of open government, one might expect fairly widespread take-up at the local level. There are other reasons why one might expect open government to have particular salience at the local level. In general, the literature on open government has frequently suggested that municipal politicians are closer to their constituents and operate in a sphere of decision-making that has greater impact on people s day to day lives. As a result, there is a sense that people can have a greater impact on decision-making at the local level. Indeed, local go- vernments are often seen as potential arenas for democratic experimentation and the development of participatory opportunities for citizen engagement. In this context, one might expect open government to be taken up in a local context more readily than it might at provincial or national levels (see for example Wainwright and MacIntosh (Eds.) 1987). At the same time, there are also reasons to expect that local government may be particularly ill suited to demo- 7 CJUR 70ThThfi1 flff:2 flffiflffi Canadian Journal of Urban Research Revue canadienne de recherche urbaine cratic experimentation. Local government is sometimes seen as particularly vulnerable to capture by vested interests, particularly property developers and local industry, which may have privileged access to government decision-makers . While this may be true of large municipalities, it may even be more relevant to small municipalities, where local elites are a far tighter and more clearly defined group of people. For small municipalities, resources and capacity to pursue open government initiatives may also be limited, particularly if there is a need for investment in technological infrastructure. An initial scan of municipal websites, however, suggested that open government had relatively little salience at the local level. A review of the 50 largest municipalities in Canada demonstrated that very few municipalities had adopted formal open government plans, and with the exception of the concept of open data, relatively few munici- palities had pursued open government themes. Table 1: Open government themes The federal government s Open Government portal seems to indicate a much broader local take-up of open government principals by municipalities. It lists 60 open municipalities ( ta-canada overlay_1). However, these municipalities have been designated as open due to the existence of some sort of data portal or data repository. This would seem to confirm the notion that open data is the preferred mecha- nism by which most municipalities pursue openness. These preliminary results led to a series of questions, which we pursue more thoroughly in this paper. Exami- ning websites tells us very little about the nature of open government initiatives, and the attitudes of local politicians and officials towards open government. Are there specific obstacles to implementing open government at the local level? Are initiatives the result of pressure from above (provincial or federal) or are they locally generated? Is the adoption of open government the result of pressure from below (citizen-led demands) or is it a bureaucratic or po- litician-led policy? In order to pursue these issues in greater detail we conducted a national survey with elected and appointed mu- nicipal officials. The intention was to generate a fuller picture of if, and how, open government was being adopted at the local level, and to develop a better understanding of both obstacles and opportunities for open government. The results, we hope, will contribute to the open government debate, and assist in developing effective open government strategies. Methodology To examine the extent to which open government strategies have been adopted at the municipal level we conducted a French and English language survey. The survey asked respondents about the existence of formal open government strategies in their municipality, the objectives of such strategies, along with details regarding how the policies were developed and implemented. A copy of the survey is included in Appendix A. 7 CJUR 70ThThfi1 flff:2 flffiflffi 3e adoption of open government by local governments in Canada: Obstacles and possibilities We invited mayors, city council members, members of city clerk s offices, and the chief administrative officers in 100 cities to participate in the survey. We cast a wide net when recruiting participants with the hopes of capturing possible variations in the initiatives present in cities of different sizes and within several provinces. Our sample in- cluded the ten most populous cities within each province. The cities were determined with the help of national and provincial data (the full list of cities can be found in the Appendix B). Although this sampling technique attemp- ted to include an equal number of cities from each province, it also led to a list of cities with extreme variations in population given that the largest city in one province (Toronto, for example) was often significantly larger than the most populous city in another (Charlottetown, for example). Despite the size discrepancies, we opted to pursue this approach in order to overcome an issue that arose in the review of municipal websites referred to above. Of the 50 largest municipalities examined in that study, 23 came from Ontario, 10 from Quebec, and 8 from British Columbia. Manitoba, by contrast, only had 1 city that made the list, and several Atlantic Canadian provinces were excluded completely. Sampling an equal number of municipalities from each province helped to overcome this limitation. We received a total of 56 responses to the English survey and 26 to the French survey, for a total of 82 responses. A majority of participants were council members, with some participants identifying as chief administrative officers, mayors, and senior policy staff. From the 56 responses in the English survey, 51 participants provided the name of the city they represent. Although our original sample targeted ten municipalities in each province, and each province was represented in our sample, responses remained skewed towards certain provinces. The most responses came from Alberta (25 ; n 13), British Columbia (22 ; n 11), Manitoba (18 ; n 9), and New Brunswick (12 ; n 6). There was only one participant that identified with a city in Ontario and only one from Nova Scotia. The French respondents were predominantly from Quebec (75 ; n 18) and New Brunswick (25 ; n 6). Overall, the survey results are quite tilted towards western Canada (particularly in the English survey), with major cities in Ontario not represented. This discrepancy was somewhat puzzling in that of the six cities possessing formal open government plans in our initial scan, three of them (Toronto, Kitchener, and Guelph) were from Ontario. It should also be noted that the three territories were not included in this research. There are several other limitations to the survey. The terms we used in our survey were not always defined. As a result, responses may reflect the individual respondent s interpretation of the term, which may be different than how the term is used in the open government literature. Very few of the terms associated with open government have definitive and clear meanings. The extent to which the survey was able to capture these variations may therefore be limited. The survey included both multiple choice, rank order, and open-ended questions. Some participants did not answer all questions and, in general, the open-ended questions were the most likely not to elicit a response. Finally, this research does not test the effectiveness of open government strategies. Our intention is to engage in a prelimi- nary investigation into the adoption of strategies and their integration at the municipal level. The results, therefore, cannot speak to the quality of the policies under investigation. Finally, surveying municipal officials may have also led to a response bias, with certain participants feeling the need to either bolster their current policies or emphasize certain aspects while not mentioning others. However, our more detailed survey of municipal politicians and officials suggested a greater awareness of open government concepts. Out of 82 participants, 54 said their municipality had an open government strategy (n 44) and 27 said they did not (n 22).
