0|dashboard  | ntifying some of the ongoing issues around public participation and local gover- nance in Canada, and by exploring its impact on local democracy. 2.1 Period 1: The Age of Consultation Arguably, local governments in Canada have been at the vanguard of public par- ticipation by all levels of government in the country. Since the 1960s, they have had to comply with requirements for public consultation on land use planning matters. These requirements were placed on local governments by provincial governments planning legislation. This is somewhat ironic, as provincial governments did not incorporate citizen consultation into their own practice until sometime later. The federal government in Canada has also lagged behind municipalities in its own policies and practices related to citizen participation and engagement. There was, however, a second impetus for the relatively early adoption of public participation as an integral part of local government in Canada. This was the local activism of the 1960s and early 1970s, as citizens groups mobilized to stop local mega-development plans for expressways, skyscrapers, and other forms of urban renewal. Although these protests were not always successful, they did inculcate the practice in most Canadian municipalities of at least informing citizens of their local government s intentions before putting shovels in the ground, altering community programs, and making budget decisions. At least initially, political officials and administrative staff in many municipalities undertook even the most basic forms of consultation reluctantly. The thought of actually meeting with residents who might object to planning proposals was repugnant to councillors who, at least in the City of Toronto, were widely described as the old guard . The need for consultation and its attendant practices moved further onto cen- ter stage in Canadian municipalities in the 1960s as a result of heightened social activism in the period and as a result of conflicting views about urban development and livable cities. Jane Jacobs seminal work, The Death and Life of Great American Cities, was published in 1961. Her ideas played a significant part in energizing one of the touchstone examples of urban activism during this period, the fight to stop a proposed Spadina Expressway that would tear out established neighborhoods in the core of Toronto. The forces for and against the expressway waged political battle for years. Resolution of the issue finally occurred when the provincial government stepped in in the early 1970s to cancel the project . But, the engage- ment and demands to be heard were essentially local, contributing, among other 16 Citizen Participation at the Local Level in China and Canada things, to the 1972 election of a reform-minded council in the City of Toronto, under Mayor David Crombie. That council took consultation and controversy to new heights, in part due to its plan to limit the height of buildings on the down- town core to 45 feet. It is somewhat ironic that a federal government initiative fueled local demands for voice in cities and town halls in Canada during this period. The Company of Young Canadians was established in the 1960s, modeled roughly as a Canadian domestic version of John F. Kennedy s Peace Corps. The federal govern- ment funded young people to become community developers, living and work- ing for social justice in communities big and small across Canada. CYC members were active in various community development and antidevelopment initiatives in Canadian municipalities, including, for example, in the City of Montreal, which had many specific neighborhood struggles during this period, played out against a tradition of machine politics in city hall . Although rooted in land use planning, expectation that consultations would occur expanded into other realms of municipal government activity, ranging from budgeting to community services programming to regulation of the local taxi industry. Two main instruments for local government consultation emerged dur- ing this period. The first and perhaps most prevalent is the public meeting or information ses- sion. These meetings may be attended and hosted by local politicians and municipal staff. Typically, there is a presentation (often with visual aids maps, charts, etc.), a question and answer period, and an informal conclusion. Some municipalities employ professional facilitators to chair these sessions, giving rise to a cadre of public participation professionals who are preoccupied only with process and not with substantive issues. Experience with these meetings varies dramatically. officials vastly outnumber public attendees. In other cases, when the issue is par- ticularly hot, the audience can number in the hundreds. Typically this occurs when a proposed development or service change is thought to negatively affect residents. On planning issues, the not in my backyard sentiment may be very strongly expressed on these occasions. Although use of this format to engage citizens remains very common, a rather cynical view of public meetings that these are really occasions to tell and sell, rather than to engage, has contributed to municipal governments adoption of other engagement practices. It must be said, however, that the public meeting remains central to public par- ticipation by both local politicians and staff. Indeed, the respective roles of members of municipal council and staff officials in calling and participating in public meet- ings have sometimes been a source of friction between them. For example, the 2 Task Force on Good Governance in the City of Ottawa heard complaints from councillors in that city that staff were active in their wards without their knowledge. The second instrument that emerged in the early period of consultation and which remains a cornerstone of engagement in many Canadian municipalities The Paradox of Participation 17 is the advisory committee. In the early 1970s, the newly amalgamated City of Winnipeg created Resident Advisory Groups to be consulted and provide Les conseils de quartier, established in Quebec in the early 1990s, served the same function, representing the views and aspirations of neighborhood residents to the city council. Other advisory committees are focused For example, as of 2013, the City of Ottawa had five advisory committees, including the Advisory Committee on Disabilities, whose focus is to make the city more accessible, and the Environmental Stewardship Advisory Committee to advise council on policy, programs, and services related to environmental stewardship. This latter committee includes eight members of the public plus one member of council (Ottawa.ca en city-hall your-city-government advisory-committees). Citizen members are individuals who have a direct interest in the service or policy area as either a consumer or a provider. The municipal council remains firmly in charge. In addition to these two standard operating procedures for citizen participa- tion, we also see the seeds of richer engagement practices emerging in this early period. In the late 1960s, the federal government launched the Neighborhood Improvement Program . As the name suggests, the program provided funds for the improvement of neighborhoods in cities across the country. An important innovation was that active consultation had to occur between municipal officials and neighborhood residents. A mutually agreeable plan and priorities for improve- ment had to exist before federal funds would flow. Just as with planning legislation, the early roots of more complex citizen engagement by municipal government lay in the actions of another level of government. 2.2 Period 2: Engagement by Necessity Beginning in the 1990s, municipal governments in Canada found themselves deal- ing with three major challenges: First was the realization that there was a need to deal more broadly with issues related to the urban environment than through the lens of land use planning. The second was the challenge of municipal restructuring, generally through the amalgamation of several municipalities into one larger entity. Restructuring affected municipal governments and communities large and small in a number of Canadian provinces. Finally, municipal governments were thrust into the world of alternative service delivery and disengagement from servicing. This has occurred by both design and necessity. Each of these challenges contributed to new forms of public participation and, in some cases, conflict. The GoPlan exercise undertaken by the City of Calgary in the 1990s pro- vides a good example of a municipality engaging citizens to respond to a broadly conceived environmental challenge. GoPlan attempted to find more comprehen- sive and effective ways to engage stakeholders around environmental sustain- ability in the face of rivershed damage, urban encroachment on arable farmland, 18 Citizen Participation at the Local Level in China and Canada air pollution, and traffic issues . The city engaged a well- established network of neighborhood community associations in this planning exercise but expanded process to include a roundtable working group of city offi- cials, developers, school boards, the local university, and the building industry, as well as community associations. There were also designated advisors to the roundtable from the health and social service sectors, as well as the real estate industry. Opportunities for participation by the general public were very extensive and accompanied by widespread media publicity. There were many public meet- ings, open houses, and discussion papers produced for discussion and debate. In their review of the process, Jamieson . conclude that it contributed to the development of comprehensive policies consistent with the needs that drove the exercise. Somewhat ironically, this successful process was not retained as a permanent part of the city s policy process. Even with its apparent success, it was subject to criticism for its cost and the view in some quarters that it was a public relations circus. During this period, nothing aroused more passionate engagement than the Ideology and the quest for cost savings and efficiencies propelled municipal governments and their citizens into heated This occurred in a number of provinces, including Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, and Ontario. Beginning in the 1990s, the provincial government in Ontario embarked on an amalgamation crusade that saw the total number of municipalities in the prov- ince reduced by almost one-half. In some cases, these were forced marriages of municipalities who came together voluntarily to avoid the provincial government dictating their fate. In other cases, provincial governments took preemptive steps by appointing restructuring commissioners to consider options. Regardless of the process, there was considerable citizen debate and engagement. Perhaps the most celebrated case of public participation around restructuring occurred in connection with the Ontario government s 1996 decision to step into discussions being held at the municipal level around restructuring in the City of Toronto by disbanding the existing two-tier metropolitan government system that had existed since the 1950s and replacing it with a single amalgamated mega-city. Aside from the political opposition expressed by five of the six lower-tier mayors and councils, one could only describe the ensuing months as being characterized by mass mobilization against amalgamation. A former mayor of the City of Toronto spearheaded an organization called Citizens for Local Democracy (C4LD) that consistently drew about 1200 people out to weekly Monday night meetings in opposition to the amalgamation. C4LD also made innovative use of the Internet and listservs to keep people informed. Four citizens organizations and 125 individ- uals came together to form Citizens Legal Challenge Inc. in order to do just that challenge the provincial legislation to create the new city. This group was ultimately unsuccessful, including in its attempt to have its case heard by the Supreme Court of Canada (Moore Milroy 2003). The Paradox of Participation 1 Toronto was not the only case of passionate engagement around amalga- mation. There was equal heat surrounding amalgamation (and subsequent de- amalgamation) in Montreal, in the City of Halifax, and in more rural locations. In at least one case, a provincial appointee charged with considering restructuring required police protection because emotions ran so high. The third impetus for changes in the public participation process during this period was necessitated by a significant retrenchment by different levels of govern- ment in the delivery of services. Although local governments in Canada already had a much more extensive background in contracting out services both to the private sector and to community groups than either the federal or provin- cial governments, the rise of the doctrine of new public management in North America in the 1990s led to more active exploration of the possibilities of using either the private or voluntary sectors to provide alternative service delivery. Simultaneously, municipal governments found themselves hit by severe financial cutbacks by the federal government and provinces. Municipalities were called upon to take on new responsibilities and, in some cases, had to divest themselves of tradi- tional activities as their financial situation grew more dire. Debates about alterna- tive service delivery at the local level, especially regarding P3s, became more heated. Two possible reasons are the intensity of financial stress local governments were experiencing and the vocal opposition to P3s as they were contemplated by all levels of government. Organized labor was frequently in the vanguard of this opposition. From a public participation perspective, there were three main results. First, lines of accountability for local services and budget choices became more com- plex. If citizens were unhappy with the quality of local garbage collection, who was accountable city hall or the private contractor hired by city hall? Second, pressures to choose priorities among municipal services and in some cases to trim or cut services during this time contributed to the rise of new approaches to assessing citizens needs and preferences. A number of municipali- ties (for example, the City of Brockville and the City of Burlington) began to use citizen surveys. These surveys attempted to measure three things: the familiarity and use of various local services by residents, their satisfaction with the service provided, and the priority they would attach to having the service available (at vary- ing levels of service) in the future. In a number of municipalities citizens became involved in either advising on the entire municipal budget (Burlington see Fenn 1998, Edmonton see LeSage 1998) or allocating small parts of it (Guelph see Learner and Van Wagner 2006). The third result was that municipal governments in Canada became even more engaged with local voluntary organizations. During this period, the character of the voluntary sector in municipalities across Canada was changing especially in the large cities. The population of Canada s cities was becoming increasingly diverse with the resulting rise of new organizations to provide services to assist different groups, regardless of where they happened to reside in the city. Civil society organi- zations in Canadian cities now reflect a community of interest (born out of ethnic 20 Citizen Participation at the Local Level in China and Canada identity, gender, economic status) as much as they reflect geographic communities within the city. In some cases, local voluntary organizations (both interest based and geograph- ically based) were contracted to perform activities previously undertaken directly by the municipality. In other cases, the voluntary sector found itself under pressure to assume responsibility for services from which the municipality had completely withdrawn (often as a result of downloading and offloading from other levels of government). The representative and service functions provided by an increasing array of local voluntary organizations during this period made them increasingly visible forces at city halls across the country. The result has been a more complex corporatist approach to policy making and service delivery in Canadian municipal government. For example, the delivery of services to homeless people by the City of Hamilton has been guided by a community action plan, developed by a coalition through the city s Social Planning Council. Furthermore, allocation of the city s homeless project funds has been undertaken by a volunteer community advisory board . 2.3 Period 3: Shared Government Perhaps as a logical extension of the emergence of a more complex constellation of local constituencies and the struggles for local economic and social health that occurred with the download of the 1990s, there are now signs of a new paradigm of public participation with municipal government in Canada. This is founded on a collaborative model involving local governments, the private sector, and local vol- untary organizations, as well as active citizens, in moving the local public agenda forward. The elements are deceptively simple assessing where the locality is, where it wants to go, and how to get there. The process involves many local orga- nizations, of which municipal government is just one, with a defined niched role. Other sectors and other governments are seen as having their niches as well. The City of Ottawa offers up at least two examples. The City for All Women Initiative describes itself as a partnership between women from diverse communities, organizations, academics and the City of Ottawa ( ivtf.org). CAWI has actively engaged city council on its budget plans. It has also developed a diversity lens to assist the city in assessing the responsiveness of vari- ous policies to the diversity of the community. The Ottawa Centre for Research and Innovation was founded approximately 20 years ago, principally as an advocacy group for the high-technology sector in the region. It has metamorphosed into the area s principal economic planning and development organization, involv- ing local municipalities, universities, colleges and school boards, and the private sector ( The engagement of citizens is done through the municipality and by other means. For example, in the City of Toronto, the development of a contemporary The Paradox of Participation 21 situation analysis for the city government occurred through its Listening to Toronto initiative. Beginning in 2003, the city, through its mayor and council, consulted Torontonians about what citywide issues they viewed as important and what they would recommend to address them. The initiative was guided by an explicit set of principles: The city would seek advice on citywide topics where public advice is wanted and needed. The decision makers would be in the room, listening. Participants would be provided with good information about the topic at hand. The diversity of the city would be reflected in those who participate (http: Simultaneously, the volunteer philanthropic organization the Community Foundation of Toronto has been issuing an annual community report card in which volunteer raters assess the city s economic, social, and population health and issues to be addressed. Further, the Toronto City Summit convened municipal and community leaders to identify and deal with pressing issues facing the city. There is no shortage of engagement on the analysis, and the city government is one of many players. Similarly, responsibility for engagement around action is shared. Although identity-based interest groups are recognized, proponents of this new approach to community development argue that, ultimately, engagement must be about place. The communities agenda is about local expression within a shared understand- ing . The most comprehensive locally based initiative that reflects this new paradigm is Vibrant Communities a community-driven effort to reduce poverty by engag- ing people, community-based organizations, businesses, and governments in locali- ties across Canada. In each community, four key approaches are used: Comprehensive local initiatives aimed at poverty reduction Grassroots collaboration involving all sectors of the community Identifying community assets and putting them to good use in poverty reduction efforts A commitment to learning, change, and sharing experience with both success and failure ( All of these suggest some role for local government, but one important dimen- sion of Vibrant Communities, from a public participation perspective, is the com- mitment to sharing experience among local (and other participating) governments related to success and failure on engagement. Local officials from participating municipalities have an opportunity to take part in a government learning circle for this purpose. The discussions that have occurred to date go beyond describing 22 Citizen Participation at the Local Level in China and Canada techniques for engagement among local governments and other local actors. They also examine the opportunities for and limits to public participation. It is important to realize, however, that these new approaches coexist with more traditional struggles related to citizens thinking that they are adequately heard at city hall. There are two recent cases in point in the City of Ottawa. The first con- cerns the proposed revitalization of a sports and exhibition facility in the central part of the city (Lansdowne Park). It is a site-specific planning issue. The second concerns the city s response to dissatisfaction among some of its rural residents. This has been an ongoing issue since amalgamation in 2001 of a number of municipali- ties into a 2796-square-kilometer city that incorporates large areas of agricultural and country estate property, as well as a much denser urban and suburban core. 2.3.1 Lansdowne Live In 2 Ottawa City Council voted to initiate a design competition to revitalize Lansdowne Park, an exposition site in the central city. The site also contained a der- elict stadium. It is in the midst of a well-established and prosperous mixed neigh- borhood and abuts the Rideau Canal, a UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site. Announcement of the design competition was followed by standard public par- ticipation operating procedure: an information open house ; two public workshops, attended by individuals, community organizations, the local councilor, and city staff ; and a survey sent to indi- viduals who had registered to participate in the city s deliberations . But, both the process and the potential outcome became the subject of considerable controversy. It ultimately ended in the courts. The city put the design competition on hold in late 2008 after receiving an unsolicited bid from a consortium of local developers (the Ottawa Sports and Entertainment Group ) to rebuild the stadium (with the city bearing the estimated 75 million cost) to house a football team, for which OSEG had a con- ditional franchise, and add a mixed-use development consisting of retail, high- rise condominiums, and a hotel. A second stadium proposal (again unsolicited) in another part of the city complicated the picture. During the third week of April 2009, the City of Ottawa Planning Committee heard representations both for and against these unsolicited proposals. Most attention was focused on the Lansdowne proposal. Local businesses and residents were worried about the design and impact on traffic and existing neighborhoods. Online commentary on news reports of the unfolding story was active. The local councillor was opposed to the process being used and to the development concept itself. He tried, among other things, to have council revert to the original design competition and to have his colleagues on council declare whether they had received election funding from the proponent The author was privileged to be a co-facilitator of this group in 2007. The Paradox of Participation 23 developers or their employees. On April 23, 2009, council voted 14 to 9 to proceed with a 60-day exclusive negotiation on the Lansdowne Live proposal. A number of conditions, at least partly intended to reflect the concerns of critics of the proposal in its current form, were attached to moving forward. A revised proposal was unveiled for public and council consideration in autumn 2009. A series of public consultations were held across the city. The approach taken to these consultations altered considerably as they proceeded, principally because the first session, held on the proposed development site, was widely acknowledged to be a disaster. Staff of the proponents were discovered to be wearing name badges that suggested they were city staff. The format did not allow for a question and answer session, until one irate member of the public used a bullhorn to take control of the meeting and open it up. While changes in approach did occur, it was the image of an enraged citizenry, led by a person standing on a chair with bullhorn in hand, that symbolized this part of the process . These consultations were followed by 17 hours of council debate, including submissions by 90 interveners. The amended proposal passed to the next stage of consideration in mid-November 2009. However, ongoing public debate about the design, viability of the project, and its impact on the surrounding community prompted city council to appoint an independent three-person expert design panel to review and consult on the plans for the site as they moved forward. Not to be assuaged, a group of concerned citizens, Friends of Lansdowne Park, launched cases against the proposal at the provincial oversight body for local planning, the These challenges were dismissed. Friends of Lansdowne Park then moved on to a legal challenge in September 2010. Their case was built on the assertion that the city had not engaged in a proper competitive bid- ding process. In February 2011 the Superior Court of Ontario ruled against Friends of Lansdowne. That same month, the city released a modified design for the proj- ect, emphasizing more green space and some reduction in height of the proposed high-rise buildings. Work commenced in 2012 with continued controversy about improper tree cutting on the site and the impact of excavation on surrounding buildings. Work continues with completion set for 2015. In many respects, this case exemplifies the common impact of public participa- tion on planning matters the developer carries the day, but not the whole way, as public concerns are aired in the debate. Today, these concerns are aired through formal processes such as the workshops and meetings described above and through traditional and new media. Further, this particular case illustrates that despite many years of experience with public participation, cities can get the process very wrong. This can enrage the electorate. In Ottawa, for example, the Lansdowne Live controversy contributed to an upswing of public interest in the autumn 2010 civic elections. The mayor presiding over the Lansdowne decisions was roundly defeated, as were an unusually high number of incumbent councillors. Nonetheless, the Lansdowne revitalization continues. 24 Citizen Participation at the Local Level in China and Canada 2.3.2 Keeping Rural Ottawa in the Fold The amalgamated City of Ottawa (amalgamated in 2001) had a 2011 population of approximately 883,391 ( and an area of 2796 square kilometers. Approximately 84,500 people live in four rural wards that cover 80 of the city s land mass ( Rural Ottawa contains a mix of operating farms, villages, and country residences. The majority of Ottawa s rural population relies significantly on the central city and suburbs for employment, healthcare, shopping, and other services. The rural municipalities that preexisted the amalgamated city were among the most ardent opponents to amalgamation. Rural opposition at the time resulted in the establishment of the four distinctively rural wards. Despite a proposal by a citi- zen s task force on ward boundaries in 2003 that the city s ward structure be altered to reflect the conjoined interests of rural and contiguous suburban areas, the four original rural wards have proven to be immutable. The recommendation for ward boundary change was roundly rejected by the rural councillors and by a citizens group, the Rural Alliance, that took the proposal to quasi-judicial appeal. Concern expressed by rural residents that their voice would be drowned out in the new city led to another commitment at the time of amalgamation. An Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee of Council was entrenched in the new city structure. It was to consist of the councillors from the rural wards and other council colleagues. Its mandate is to consider and make recommendations to Council on issues and programs of special interest to residents and businesses in the rural areas including villages and hamlets, particularly agriculture and its associated industries (City of Ottawa Official Plan, Schedule A). Despite these structural safeguards, there have been ongoing expressions of frus- tration with the new city from the rural sector. These have included the centraliza- tion of services in city hall, many kilometers from the rural boundaries of the city; perceived roadblocks to dividing up rural properties; the alleged inappropriateness of some bylaws to rural traditions and realities two examples relate to noise bylaws and fire permits; and a perceived lack of understanding of rural life and perspectives by city politicians and staff. A 2 Citizen Satisfaction Survey revealed consider- able disgruntlement by rural residents. The fallout from amalgamation, some cut- ting of services in rural areas in the 2004 budget, the results of the citizen survey, and broader mobilization in the rural community prompted political direction to reconceive the relationship between city hall and rural and urban Ottawa . In November 2005, the city convened its first rural summit. The two-day summit was highly interactive and, generally, deemed successful by rural participants and city officials. It came up with a number of recommenda- tions for action over the short, medium, and longer terms. Its short-term recom- mendations included 2006 budget commitments to rural needs by the city, an expanded role for the Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee of Council, strong reliance for guidance by a Rural Issues Advisory Committee, and establishment The Paradox of Participation 25 of a Rural Affairs Office in city hall, headed by a designated rural affairs officer. Medium-term recommendations focused on action related to the variety of irritants identified above. Over the longer term, the summit recommended adoption of a borough model, which would delegate some decision making from council to the rural councillors. Although the structural recommendations of the summit were implemented, other issues remained or emerged. These included the bylaw planning issues identi- fied above as well as some specific rural suburban urban flashpoints over transpor- tation and transit, budget priorities, and expansion of rural villages and hamlets. Preparation for a second summit began in early 2008. Consultation meetings were held in each of the four rural wards. The results were posted on a special Rural Connections website ( for further commentary. The Rural Summit Steering Committee, made up of representatives from a range of rural groups and communities, worked through the issues identified and grouped them into themes (governance, by-laws, permits and processes, infrastructure and services) that would be assigned to working groups at the summit (City of Ottawa 2008). Whatever positive ideas and warm feelings that might have been generated at Rural Summit II when it occurred in April 2008 ( rural_connections rural_summit_02 community_consultation index_en.html) have been dissipated by the festering debate about the long-term future of rural areas in the city. In February 2009, a council member from the central city publicly expressed his frustration at what he termed was overrepresentation of rural interests on council and the ability of rural members to coalesce and defeat urban-oriented initiatives. He subsequently hosted a forum at city hall to discuss de-amalgamation . His crie de coeur was echoed by some rural groups whose espoused long-term goal is de- amalgamation of the city. It also aroused a lively, continuing, and unresolved debate in the blogosphere (see, for example, blogs soundoff archive 2009 02 13 269953.aspx and .com 2009 02 deamalgamation-or-politics-as-usual.html). To this point in the amalgamated city s history, the process of engaging citizens of rural Ottawa (and the city as a whole) in order to give them an opportunity to air their views and an opportunity for the city to respond seems to have had a marginal impact. The two rural summits represent fairly comprehensive opportuni- ties to give voice and engage. There have been permanent structures established at the city council level and within the city s organization to improve attention and responsiveness to rural issues. But the main impact of the rural voice seems to be rural councillor voting practices on urban issues, rather than substantive response to rural concerns. Interestingly, the City of Ottawa has not put in place any benchmarking pro- cess or citizen satisfaction survey that might enable it to answer the question if it is making any real headway in rural areas. So, engagement in the media, includ- ing the blogosphere, sets the sense of the debate. A 2 Task Force on Good Governance in the City of Ottawa strongly recommended that the city adopt the 26 Citizen Participation at the Local Level in China and Canada practice of benchmarking and regular citizen surveys in order to provide more sys- tematic understanding of rural and other issues for city hall and for citizens of the city ( As a recent controversy about implemen- tation of a mandatory green bin composting program across the city illustrates, this need has not abated. Rural residents are up in arms over the fact that without consultation, they are now expected to use city-supplied green bins for their com- post, when they have traditionally had their own garden compost systems. The requirement that they have to pay the same composting fee as their urban neigh- bors has added to rural dissatisfaction. 2.4 Local Governments and Public Participation in Canada: Assessing the Field In 2006, Turnbull and Aucoin undertook a review of public engagement in policy across all three levels of government in Canada. They concluded all levels of gov- ernment tended to work from a platform of citizen consultation rather than real citizen engagement. However, they also concluded that public participation was most feasible at the local level, because of historically better participation rates in consultation exercises and because of the lower cost of undertaking public par- ticipation within the boundaries of a single municipality, as compared to a prov- ince or nationwide efforts. Their first conclusion suggests that the local approaches (community meetings, advisory committees) used in the first period identified for analysis still tend to predominate. In light of this, it is important to summarize some of the challenges that remain for local governments and public participation in Canada. The first challenge concerns the complexity of engaging citizens at the local level. On one level, it seems simple. Citizens are individuals who happen to reside in a particular municipality by choice, by chance, or by necessity. But given histori- cally low levels of participation in municipal elections in Canada, the challenge of engaging local citizens between elections becomes one of affiliation. Specifically, local governments are confronted with the need to engage both communities of interest and geographically based communities. In each case they are multiple and varied in their characteristics, including their historical willingness and preferred approaches to engagement with government. meet this challenge, especially in our growing and increasingly diverse cities, repre- sent no small task. This is particularly so if one adheres to the view that local gov- ernance is first and foremost about place. In some of Canada s most diverse cities, a significant portion of the population has no voting rights at all because they lack Canadian citizenship. In such cases, local government s engagement of newcomers without citizenship, who may have urgent needs and particular interests, becomes challenging when councillors around the table think about votes . The concept of true local citizenship becomes complex and problematic. The Paradox of Participation 2 The second challenge concerns who is responsible for the participation process. There are three issues here. First, the emerging approach to multistakeholder com- munity leadership demonstrates the potential for public participation to occur in many contexts and at many levels having an impact on local government decision making but not necessarily being driven by local government leadership. Given its legislated responsibilities for consultation on certain matters and its traditional role in consultation, how should local governments work their public participation agendas within this new paradigm? The second issue the roles of politicians and municipal staff in undertaking pub- lic participation. In her review of the state of public participation and local govern- ment in Canada, Robinson noted that most Canadian municipalities lack a broad strategy, principled, or coordinated approach. Development and implemen- tation of public participation initiatives tends to be decentralized and diverse, and possibly ad hoc. Who should take the lead and in what circumstances? When staff undertakes engagement, how and when should council members become involved in the process? Reference was made earlier to the rise of public participation profes- sionals serving local governments, either as staff or as consultants. To what extent are these people in charge of the process? Does this mean that public participation becomes more about form than substance? Ultimately, this leads to the question of whether public participation by municipalities in Canada is a means to an end (better decisions and practices) or an end in itself. The third issue concerns the techniques of consultation. As early as 1998, Gattinger wrote about the potential of the Internet for engaging citizens with local governments in Canada. The use of citizen surveys has also been discussed, as has the time-tested reliance on community meetings and advisory committees. There is obviously no definitive right way. Local governments need to be aware of the possibilities and limits to different approaches and avoid overreliance on any one particular approach. They can also benefit from nontraditional approaches as evidenced by Winnipeg s experience using public health nurses to raise awareness about economic development issues among residents of the city s core area . This brings us logically to the question of how to evaluate citizen engagement by local government in Canada. Abelson and Gauvin suggest that evalua- tion of public participation efforts is in its infancy. To the extent that evaluation is being done, they found it to be based largely on users assessment of the process, rather than any solid evaluation framework. This seems to be true, for example, in the case of Calgary s GoPlan exercise. The absence of hard data to buttress or refute dissatisfaction with the performance of the new City of Ottawa in its rural area also exemplifies this problem. Not surprisingly, Abelson and Gauvin argue that the level of effort and costs involved in citizen engagement warrant a more rigorous approach. Irvin and Stansbury suggest some key considerations in determining whether public participation is an effective policy tool, looking at the advantages and disadvantages to both citizens and government of engagement as 28 Citizen Participation at the Local Level in China and Canada it relates to the participation process per se and to policy outcomes. Nonetheless, evaluation challenges remain, in part because some public participation processes are very fluid and sometimes indeterminate. As Fielding and Couture sug- gest, sometimes there are too many roundtables and not enough end tables. In conclusion, although public participation has been a foundation of Canadian local government for decades, there are many new and ongoing challenges. Cynicism about the undertaking remains among the public and in some parts of city halls across the country. But there is also evidence of the vitality of consultation processes. Public participation between elections is an important part of local democracy in Canada. We have examples where it has shaped the course of cities significantly. The Spadina Expressway debate s impact on the 1 Toronto municipal election is the first case cited here. But public participation has not had any consistent impact on expanding the share of our population who are willing to consider the future of their locality more holistically, through participation in local democracy through the electoral process. The cases of the Lansdowne Live proposal and rural disaffec- tion in the City of Ottawa may prove to be contemporary exceptions to this pattern. Debates about these specific issues have been translated into discussions about the future direction of the city , which likely contributed to changes in Ottawa s political leadership in the 2010 election. Perhaps that is what it takes to link public participation in local government to participation at election time. Topic Overview Attitudes towards the sexuality of older adults Younger people sometimes find it difficult to accept that older people are still interested in sex. We live in a society that regards youth and beauty together and emphasises physical attractiveness as being important for sexual relationships. It may be difficult to understand how older people can find one another attractive. Many people still find it difficult to accept that their parents might continue to enjoy sex and there is a tendency for this to be generalised to all older people . This course is based on the fundamental premise that the development of sexuality is a life-long process. In Western culture, however, we have become accustomed to thinking of sexuality and sexual desire as aspects of life that develop in adolescence, peak in early adulthood, and steadily decline thereafter. Part of the assumption that older people are not interested in, and are incapable of, enjoying active sex lives is likely derived from aspects of Restrictive sexual ideology which stipulated that the primary purpose of sexual behaviour was reproduction within heterosexual marriage. Once people were beyond their reproductive years, the primary purpose of their sexuality was eliminated. Reasons Older People May Avoid Having Sex In an interview study with people aged 60-91, the top five reasons participants gave for not wanting to engage in sexual activity were: 1. Not having to deal with sexual dysfunctions; 2. Avoiding confronting an ageing body; 3. Avoiding performance anxiety; 4. Not being interested in sex; 5. Loss of a partner. Gewirtz-Meydan, A., and Ayalon, L. . Attitudes towards the sexuality of older people are changing, albeit very gradually. As the influence of Restrictive sexual ideology, with its emphasis on reproductive sexuality, has waned, the plausibility and social acceptability of both women and men enjoying a sexual life in the latter stages of the life-span has increased. The baby-boomers , born between the late 1950 s and the mid 1960 s, now in later-life, grew-up as Permissive sexual ideology, with its pleasure-centred as opposed to reproductive-centred focus, began to increasingly influence attitudes towards sexuality. Thus, the baby-boomers, now in the senior years themselves, have been more accepting of the idea that sexuality extends beyond not just young adulthood, but perhaps into the later years of life as well. Sexual Activity is Linked to Greater Life Enjoyment and Health Among Older Adults A study of people (average age -64 men, 65 women) indicated that those who reported any sexual activity in the past year had higher enjoyment of life scores than those who were not sexually active . Sexual activity among older adults is associated with good physical and mental health, well- being, relationship satisfaction, and lower levels of depression . Sexuality and Sexual Behaviour Among Older Adults As we emerge from mid-life into later adulthood, the frequency of sexual behaviour declines (For a review of the literature on sexual behaviour and function among older adults see Cameron and Santos- Iglesias, 2024; Tr en, . 2017; For a brief overview of the need for sexual health education for seniors see SIECCAN, 2020, 21-23). However, many older people remain sexually active and having positive attitudes towards sexuality and satisfactory relationships after mid-life are important factors in determining the level of sexual activity among older people. In examining and assessing sexuality in later life, there are a number of important points to consider: 1. Relatively low levels of sexual activity and interest among older people may be partially due to negative attitudes towards sexuality in later life held by the media, family members, care-givers, and older people themselves. With respect to older people themselves, it is important to recognize that they are likely to have internalized prevailing societal attitudes equating sexuality with youth which may discourage them from seeing themselves as sexual-beings. Key Point Older people may have internalized societal messages equating sexuality with youth. 2. It is also important to consider that, for example, a person who reached age 70 in 2024 grew-up before many of the significant shifts towards the acceptance of Permissive sexual ideology in the 1960s and 1970s had occurred. As a result, they developed their attitudes towards sexuality in period characterized by more Restrictive ideological perspectives. Thus, they may be more likely to have less permissive attitudes towards non-reproductive sex (e.g., oral sex, masturbation), sexual activity outside the context of marriage, and same sex sexual activity, all of which may inhibit them from expressing their sexuality. Key Point Older people are more likely to have absorbed Restrictive ideological perspectives towards sexuality as they were growing-up than younger generations. 3. The decline in the frequency of sexual activity among older people does not necessarily reflect an elimination of their need or desire for physical intimacy but rather is the result of gradual declines in the body s ability for genital response (e.g., erection, vaginal lubrication, orgasm). In other words, the frequency of sexual arousal (how often the person becomes sexually aroused) and the intensity of genital response gradually declines. See Chapter 12 of your textbook for a summary of the physical changes of aging related to sexuality. Still, it should be recognized that a sizable number of people continue to have a desire for, and be capable of, full genital response into their 80s and even their 90s. For example, a large sample study of middle-aged and elderly men and women from around the world found that \"A substantial proportion indicated that sexual activity is essential for self-esteem and to maintain a relationship and would like to remain sexually active\" (Nicolosi, Laumann, Glasser ., 2004, ). Key Point As people grow older, the frequency and intensity of genital sexual response tends to gradually decline. 4. The decline in the frequency of specific behaviours that we commonly associate with having sex (i.e. intercourse, oral sex) among older people does not necessarily lead to reduced levels of sexual satisfaction. For example, a Canadian study of married men and women aged 51 to 81 found that although those 65 and older reported a lower frequency of intercourse than did the younger respondents, the older group reported a nearly equal level of sexual satisfaction as the younger group (For a more recent reviews of the literature on sexual satisfaction among older adults see Traeem, Carvalheira, ., 2017 and Towler ., 2021). In other words, as individuals and couples grow older, sexual satisfaction becomes less dependent on the frequency of intercourse or orgasm and more dependent on a more generalized sense of physical and emotional intimacy. The importance of physical intimacy and sensuous touch for older couples may not decline at all, in fact it may increase as the couple s relationship continues to mature. Older couples may place more emphasis on non-genitally focused cuddling and massage, bathing together, ect., as a means of expressing physical sexual intimacy. The process of enhancing physical intimacy for the older couple will be facilitated if they are able to continue and build on the developmental task of earlier adulthood of developing a strong bond based on friendship and emotional closeness. Be sure to look at A Portrait of Great Sex in Chapter 13 of your textbook. It suggests that it is only with the wisdom that experience brings that we are able to fully reach our potential as sexual beings. Key Point As individuals and couples continue to mature in the later years of life, sexual satisfaction becomes more strongly associated with a generalized sense of physical and emotional intimacy rather than with the frequency of intercourse. 5. Reduced sexual desire and interest in sexual activity among older people is often related to age associated health problems such as arthritis, stroke, various forms of cancer, and cardiovascular disease. Physical limitations, reduced energy, medication side effects, and depression often have a significant impact on a person s sexuality. The ability to maintain a self-image as a sexual-being in the face of these obstacles will, for some people, enhance their ability to accommodate these age related changes in health status and improve their overall sense of well-being. Key Point Age related changes in health status often negatively impact on sexuality. Maintaining self- image as a sexual-being can improve overall sense of well-being among older people. 6. For both women and men, mid to later life brings biological changes that impact on sexuality. For women, menopause (the cessation of menstruation) can have both physical and psychological implications for sexuality. However, as discussed in your textbook, most women are able to adapt to the changes of menopause and continue to enjoy sexual activity in the postmenopausal years. For men, andropause (the gradual, consistent decline in testosterone) can negatively impact on levels of sexual desire and function. As with women, most men are able to adapt to these biological changes and continue to have active sex lives. Key Point Most women and men are able to adapt to the biological changes brought on by menopause and andropause and continue to enjoy sexual activity. 7. The decline in the frequency of sexual activity among older people is often the result of the death of a life partner. This problem disproportionately affects women, who more often than not, outlive their male spouses. Key Point Reduced sexual activity among older people is often the result of the death of a partner. 8. The decline in the frequency of sexual activity among older people is, in many cases, due, in part, to changes in living arrangements that reduce privacy. For example, as discussed below, people living in long-term care facilities such as nursing homes often lack sufficient privacy to engage in sexual activity. Key Point Reduced sexual activity among older people can be due, in part, to reduced privacy associated with changes in living arrangements. 9. Although Western culture is increasing recognizing the right of older people to express and enjoy their sexuality, it also important to accept that, for a variety of reasons, for many older people, sexual expression is no longer a priority. Indeed, as we have seen in this course, contemporary society places considerable pressure on individuals to maintain high standards of sexual attractiveness and sexual functioning. Some people, as the enter the later stages of life, will feel a sense of freedom as a result of no longer being subjected to the pressure to meet these standards. Key Point Promoting the right of older people to express and enjoy their sexuality should be balanced with the recognition that for some people, freedom from the pressures associated with maintaining an active sex life will be welcomed. Developmental Tasks Related to Sexuality in Later Life Consideration of the above points enables us to pinpoint the major developmental tasks related to sexuality in later life. Maintaining one s self-perception as a sexual being in a culture that equates sexuality with youth. Continued progression of the developmental tasks of early and middle adulthood including balanced integration of passion and friendships in romantic sexual relationships. Adapting to a reduction in the frequency and intensity of genital sexual response while maintaining physical intimacy. Adapting to changing life circumstances such as loss of a partner and or entry into a long-term care facility (e.g., nursing home). The Importance of Sex: Comments from Older People. The 2019 edition of the Canadian Guidelines for Sexual Health Education suggests that organizations that serve seniors should provide their clients with access to sexual health education and services and that personal working in these facilities should be given opportunities for \"in-service and continuing education to increase their capacity to provide effective comprehensive sexual health education to seniors, including LGBTQ2S seniors, and should include training to connect seniors to appropriate sexual health services\" (SIECCAN, 2019, ; See also SIECCAN, 2020, pages 73-74). Research indicates that the majority of senior home residents, both with and without dementia, attach at least some level of importance to sexuality in their lives and some of them engage in a range of sexual activities including masturbation, use of sexually explicit materials, kissing, touching, and intercourse . In a recent survey of U.S. nursing home directors of nursing, 71 reported that there had been issues regarding residents sexual activities (Lester, Kohen, Stefanacci and Feuerman, 2016). As Hajjar and Kamel suggest, A long-term care facility can make all the difference between residents achieving a fulfilling and therapeutic sex life, or becoming frustrated at attempting to do so (). Historically, promoting sexual health and providing an environment conducive to sexual expression has been a low priority for nursing home administrations and staff. Indeed, in many nursing homes, sexual expression has been, and continues to be, actively discouraged. Key Point In many cases, nursing homes ignore the sexuality needs of residents or actively discourage sexual expression. Although sexuality and sexual expression may not be a relevant priority for many nursing home residents, for others, it will continue to play a role in contributing to their overall well-being. However, there are a number of obstacles to sexual expression faced by nursing home residents. These include: Lack of privacy: Many nursing home residents do not have private bedrooms or access to private spaces where sexual activity is possible, appropriate or comfortable. Family attitudes: Children of nursing home residents may be uncomfortable acknowledging or addressing the sexuality needs of their parent(s), particularly if a parent has formed a new relationship at the nursing home. Staff attitudes: Nursing home administration and staff may approach and view resident sexual behaviour negatively, seeing it as a source of problems, rather than approaching it in a positive way, seeing it as an expression of residents need for physical intimacy.
